blocks.html: In Total and Marginal Utility you counted "utils" as if satisfaction came in units you could add up. Intermediate microeconomics starts one step earlier and asks for much less. All we assume is that a person can rank bundles of goods: for any two bundles A and B, she can say which she prefers, or that she likes them equally. Everything else in consumer theory, from demand curves to welfare measures, is built on top of that ranking.

A bundle is a list of amounts, such as $(x, y) = (3, 5)$: 3 units of good $x$ and 5 of good $y$. We write $A \succ B$ for "A is preferred to B," $A \sim B$ for "A and B are equally good" (indifference), and $A \succeq B$ for "A is at least as good as B."

Preferences are rational when they are complete (any two bundles can be compared) and transitive (if $A \succeq B$ and $B \succeq C$, then $A \succeq C$). Two more assumptions give the usual shapes: more is better (monotonicity: more of a good, with no less of anything, is preferred) and convexity (a taste for variety: a mix of two equally good bundles is at least as good as either one).

Completeness and transitivity are what let us line every bundle up in one consistent order, with ties allowed. Without transitivity the order can loop: if $A \succ B$, $B \succ C$ and $C \succ A$, there is no "best" bundle, and a trader could charge you a small fee to swap C for B, then B for A, then A for C, and walk you around the circle forever. More-is-better makes indifference curves slope down, because to stay equally happy with more of one good you must give up some of the other. Convexity makes them bow toward the origin: people usually prefer a balanced mix to extremes.

Compare B and C: the same story, one good up and one down. Undecided.

blocks.title: Chaining with transitivity
blocks.q: For Omar, $A \succ B$, $B \sim C$ and $C \succ D$. How does A compare with D?
steps: From $A \succ B$ and $B \sim C$: transitivity gives $A \succ C$ (a strict link keeps the chain strict).

blocks.html: Thinking "rational" means selfish or sensible. The axioms say nothing about what a person likes. Someone who would rather give \$50 to a food bank than spend it on herself, or who prefers sweets to vegetables, can have perfectly rational preferences. Rationality here means only that the rankings are complete and consistent. Check: when you are tempted to call a preference irrational, ask whether it breaks completeness or transitivity. If it doesn't, it is rational in the economist's sense.

These axioms are a model, and a useful one. Behavioral economics studies where real choices depart from them, for example when the way an option is framed changes which one people pick. Economists broadly agree the axioms are a good starting point; how much the departures matter for a given question is studied case by case.

blocks.html: Once a person can rank bundles, we can draw the ranking. Fix one bundle and collect every bundle she likes exactly as much. That set is an indifference curve. If her preferences come from a utility function $U(x, y)$, the curve is the graph of the equation $U(x, y) = k$, just as in A Graph Shows Every Solution: every point on it satisfies the equation, and no other point does.

An indifference curve is a set of bundles with equal utility, $U(x, y) = k$. Under the usual assumptions the curves slope down, never cross, fill the whole graph (one through every bundle), and curves farther from the origin are preferred.

Down-sloping: start at a bundle and add some $x$. Under more-is-better that is an improvement, so to get back to the same level you must take some $y$ away. Never crossing: suppose two curves met at bundle C. Pick A on the higher curve and B on the lower one. Then $A \sim C$ and $C \sim B$, so by transitivity $A \sim B$, even though A sits on the higher curve and is strictly preferred. That contradiction means curves of one person cannot cross. One through every bundle: completeness lets every bundle be compared with every other, so each one has its own set of equally good bundles.

And a bundle on a higher curve can contain less of one good, as B did. Check: to compare two bundles, compute their utilities (or find their curves). Only when one bundle has more of both goods can you rank them without the curves.
Indifference curves are the consumer's side of the picture. In Budget Sets we add what she can afford, and in The Best Affordable Bundle we put the two together.

blocks.html: An indifference map can be summarized by a single function. A utility function $U(x, y)$ gives each bundle a number so that preferred bundles get bigger numbers: $U(A) > U(B)$ exactly when $A \succ B$, and $U(A) = U(B)$ exactly when $A \sim B$. Its level curves are the Indifference Curves.

Utility is ordinal: only the ranking it gives matters, not the size of the numbers. If $f$ is any strictly increasing function, $V = f(U)$ describes exactly the same preferences, as with Composition of Functions: feed $U$'s output into $f$.

For an increasing $f$, $U(A) > U(B)$ if and only if $f(U(A)) > f(U(B))$, and equal inputs give equal outputs. So $V = f(U)$ ranks every pair of bundles the same way as $U$. Its level curves are the same curves with new labels: the curve $U = 6$ is the curve $V = f(6)$. A decreasing $f$ (such as $f(u) = -u$ or $1/u$) flips every ranking, so it describes opposite preferences.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: $U = xy$ as a surface. The contour lines on the floor are the indifference curves. $\ln U = \ln x + \ln y$ or $(xy)^2$ would make a surface of a different height and shape, but with the same contour lines in the same order.

blocks.title: Which functions describe the same preferences?
blocks.q: $U(x, y) = xy$ for $x, y > 0$. Do these describe the same preferences? $V_1 = \ln x + \ln y$, $V_2 = 3xy + 5$, $V_3 = -xy$, $V_4 = x + y$.
steps: $V_1 = \ln(xy) = \ln U$, and $\ln$ is increasing: same preferences.
$V_3 = -U$ is decreasing in $U$: it reverses every ranking.
$V_4$ is not a function of $U$ at all. For example $(1, 9)$ and $(3, 3)$ have $V_4 = 10$ and $6$, but $U = 9$ for both: $V_4$ ranks a pair that $U$ calls a tie.

blocks.title: Same curve, new label
blocks.q: Kara's preferences are described by $U = xy$ and by $V = 2(xy)^2 + 1$. Which level of V is the indifference curve $U = 5$?
steps: Write V in terms of U: $V = 2U^2 + 1$.
Same bundles, same curve; only the label changed.

blocks.html: Treating utility as measured happiness. If $U(A) = 20$ and $U(B) = 10$, it is tempting to say A is "twice as good." But $V = \ln U$ describes the same person with values about 3.0 and 2.3, and $V = U^3$ gives 8,000 and 1,000. The ratio means nothing; only the order does. Check: a statement about preferences is meaningful only if every increasing transformation of $U$ leaves it true.

Ordinal utility is all we need for choices without risk. When we compare risky prospects in Expected Utility, the scale matters more: there a utility function is pinned down up to a positive linear change $aU + b$ with $a > 0$.

blocks.html: In Total and Marginal Utility marginal utility was the change in total utility from one more unit, read off a table. With a smooth utility function we can do better and find the rate at an exact bundle. The tool is the partial derivative from Partial Derivatives: change one good a little, hold the other fixed, and see how fast $U$ rises.

$$MU_x = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}, \qquad MU_y = \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}.$$ $MU_x$ is the extra utility per unit of a small increase in $x$, with $y$ held where it is. A small change $\Delta x$ raises utility by about $MU_x\,\Delta x$.

The table version is a difference quotient, $\Delta U/\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = 1$. Shrink the step and the quotient settles on a limit: $\displaystyle \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{U(x + h, y) - U(x, y)}{h}$. That limit is the partial derivative. Because $y$ stays fixed, you differentiate as if $y$ were a number: a factor of $y$ rides along, and a term with only $y$ in it drops out.

blocks.name: surface
blocks.cap: $U = \sqrt{xy}$ cut by the plane $y = 4$. The trace is $U = 2\sqrt{x}$, a curve in $x$ alone. Its slope at each $x$ is $MU_x$ at that bundle, and it flattens as $x$ grows: diminishing marginal utility of $x$.

blocks.title: A Cobb-Douglas utility
steps: So a little more $x$ (say 0.1 unit) adds about $0.075$ to utility, and a little more $y$ adds about $0.033$.

blocks.title: A product with a shift
blocks.q: $U(x, y) = (x + 2)y$. Find $MU_x$ and $MU_y$ at $(3, 5)$.
steps: $MU_x = y$ (the factor $y$ rides along; the derivative of $x + 2$ is 1).

blocks.html: Differentiating with respect to both goods at once, or setting the other good to zero. For $U = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$, setting $y = 0$ makes $U = 0$ for every $x$, so you would wrongly find $MU_x = 0$. The other good is held fixed at its actual value, not removed. Check: your $MU_x$ should usually still contain $y$, and plugging in the bundle should give a positive number when more of $x$ helps.

Diminishing marginal utility, $\partial^2 U/\partial x^2 < 0$, is a property of the particular utility function, not of the preferences. $U = xy$ has constant $MU_x = y$, and $V = (xy)^2$ has rising $MU_x = 2xy^2$, yet both describe the same person. What survives every increasing transformation is the ratio of marginal utilities, the subject of The Marginal Rate of Substitution.

blocks.html: How much of one good would a person give up to get a little more of the other? That trade-off rate is the most important number in consumer theory. It comes from Marginal Utility as a Partial Derivative and is the slope of an indifference curve, which you can find with Implicit Differentiation.

The marginal rate of substitution is $$MRS = \frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = -\frac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{U \text{ fixed}}.$$ It is the amount of $y$ a person would give up for one more (small) unit of $x$ and stay equally well off: the size of the indifference curve's slope at that bundle.

Along an indifference curve $U(x, y) = k$, $y$ is a function of $x$. Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $$\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx} = 0, \quad\text{so}\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}.$$ In words: giving up $\Delta y$ costs about $MU_y\,|\Delta y|$ in utility, and getting $\Delta x$ adds about $MU_x\,\Delta x$. Staying on the curve means the two match, so $|\Delta y|/\Delta x = MU_x/MU_y$.

blocks.cap: For $U = \sqrt{xy}$, $MRS = y/x$. At (2, 18) she would give up 9 units of $y$ per unit of $x$; at (6, 6), only 1; at (18, 2), about 0.11. The more $x$ she has, the less $y$ she will give up for more of it: a diminishing MRS, which is what convexity means.

steps: At $(3, 1)$: $MRS = \dfrac{2}{9}$. She would give up about $2/9$ of a unit of $y$ for one more small unit of $x$.

steps: The MRS does not depend on $y$, so it is also $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $(16, 30)$.

blocks.title: The MRS survives a transformation

steps: That matches U's MRS. In general $V = f(U)$ multiplies both marginal utilities by $f'(U)$, which cancels in the ratio.

blocks.html: Writing $MU_y/MU_x$ instead of $MU_x/MU_y$, or treating the MRS as one fixed number for a curved indifference curve. Keep the good on the horizontal axis on top: the MRS of $x$ for $y$ asks how much $y$ one unit of $x$ is worth. And unless the curve is a straight line, the MRS changes from bundle to bundle, so always say where you computed it. Check: when a person has a lot of $x$ and little $y$, her MRS should be small.

blocks.html: Four utility functions cover most of what you will meet, and each has an MRS (from The Marginal Rate of Substitution) that explains its shape. Learning these four shapes now saves trouble later, because the rule for the best bundle depends on which one you face.

blocks.html: Substitutes trade at a fixed rate, so their curves are straight lines. Complements are used in fixed proportions, so their curves are L-shaped with a corner where $ax = by$. Cobb-Douglas curves are smooth and bowed with an MRS that falls as $x/y$ rises. Quasilinear curves have an MRS that depends only on $x$.

Each shape comes straight from the MRS. A constant MRS means a constant slope: a line. For complements, extra $x$ beyond the corner adds nothing (the min is set by $y$), so the curve runs flat to the right of the corner and straight up above it. For Cobb-Douglas the MRS is proportional to $y/x$: steep where $y$ is plentiful, flat where $x$ is. For quasilinear utility, $MU_y = 1$ and $MU_x = v'(x)$, so the slope at a given $x$ is the same on every curve: each curve is the one below it shifted up.

For $(14, 5)$: $\min\{14, 10\} = 10$. The 4 extra units of $x$ add nothing; $(14, 5)$ lies on the flat arm of the same curve.

blocks.html: Expecting every indifference curve to be smooth and bowed, and so applying "MRS = price ratio" everywhere. With perfect substitutes the MRS never changes, so it usually never equals the price ratio, and the best choice is a corner (all of one good). With perfect complements the MRS doesn't exist at the corner where the best choice sits. Check: before setting MRS equal to anything, identify the family. Corners and Kinks shows what to do instead.

blocks.html: Budget Constraints drew a budget line from income and two prices. Now we treat it as a set of points, the way Linear Inequalities in Two Variables treats a half-plane, and ask how taxes, discounts and limits reshape it.

With income $m$ and prices $p_1, p_2$, the budget set is every bundle with $$p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 \le m, \quad x_1, x_2 \ge 0.$$ Its boundary, the budget line, has intercepts $m/p_1$ and $m/p_2$ and slope $-p_1/p_2$. A change in one price rotates the line around the other intercept; a change in income shifts it in parallel.

The slope is an opportunity cost. Giving up one unit of good 1 frees $p_1$ dollars, which buys $p_1/p_2$ units of good 2. So the market lets you trade good 1 for good 2 at the rate $p_1/p_2$, which is the size of the line's slope. If $p_1$ rises, the most good 1 you can buy, $m/p_1$, falls, but the most good 2 you can buy, $m/p_2$, does not change: the line swings around its intercept on the good-2 axis. If income rises, both intercepts grow by the same factor and the slope stays put. And if all prices and income are multiplied by the same number, every term of $p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 \le m$ scales together, so the set doesn't change at all.

blocks.name: ec-choice
blocks.cap: Books cost \$4 and movies \$3 with \$60 to spend. When books rise to \$6, the line rotates around the movie intercept (20 movies). Bundle A (6, 10) costs \$54 before and \$66 after: affordable before, not after.

blocks.title: Intercepts, slope and a price change
blocks.q: Rosa has \$60; books cost \$4 and movies \$3. Find the intercepts and slope, then the new book intercept when books cost \$6.
steps: Slope: $-p_1/p_2 = -4/3$. Each book costs $4/3$ of a movie.
At \$6 a book, the books intercept is $60/6 = 10$; the movies intercept stays at 20.
blocks.a: Intercepts 15 and 20, slope $-4/3$; after the change the books intercept is 10.

blocks.title: A per-unit tax above a quantity (a kinked budget)
blocks.q: Rosa's city adds a \$2 tax on each book beyond the first 5. With \$60, books at \$4 and movies at \$3, what is the most books she can buy?
steps: Each book after that costs $4 + 2 = 6$ dollars. The remaining \$40 buys $40/6 = 6\tfrac{2}{3}$ more.
Most books: $5 + 6\tfrac{2}{3} = 11\tfrac{2}{3}$. The budget line is steeper ($-6/3 = -2$) to the right of $x = 5$: a kink.

blocks.html: Shifting the whole line in parallel when one price changes. A parallel shift means both intercepts move by the same proportion, which is what an income change does. When only the price of good 1 changes, the good-2 intercept $m/p_2$ cannot move. Check: recompute both intercepts after any change. If only one moved, the line rotated.

items: Income up: parallel shift out. Income down: parallel shift in.
$p_1$ up: rotates inward around the $x_2$-intercept. $p_1$ down: rotates outward.
A per-unit tax on good 1: like a higher $p_1$. A tax only above some quantity: a kink.
Rationing (at most $r$ units of good 1): cuts off the set at $x_1 = r$.

blocks.html: Put the two halves of the consumer's problem together: what she would like (her The Marginal Rate of Substitution) and what she can afford (the Budget Sets). The best affordable bundle is the point of the budget set on the highest indifference curve. With calculus it is a constrained version of Optimization.

At an interior optimum (some of both goods, smooth curves), $$MRS = \frac{MU_x}{MU_y} = \frac{p_1}{p_2} \quad\text{and}\quad p_1x + p_2y = m.$$ Equivalently, $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_1} = \dfrac{MU_y}{p_2}$: the last dollar spent on each good adds the same utility.

The MRS is what one more unit of $x$ is worth to her, in units of $y$. The price ratio is what it costs, in units of $y$. If $MRS > p_1/p_2$, she can give up $p_1/p_2$ units of $y$ to buy one more $x$, which she values at more than that: utility rises, so she should keep moving toward more $x$. If $MRS < p_1/p_2$, the reverse. Only where the two are equal does no small move along the budget line help. In calculus terms: substitute $y = (m - p_1x)/p_2$ into $U$ and differentiate with the chain rule: $$\frac{d}{dx}U\!\left(x, \frac{m - p_1x}{p_2}\right) = MU_x - \frac{p_1}{p_2}MU_y = 0.$$

blocks.html: Setting the MRS equal to $p_2/p_1$, or finding a tangency point that is not on the budget line. The MRS has $MU_x$ on top and the price ratio must have $p_1$ (the price of $x$) on top too: both are "units of $y$ per unit of $x$." And the tangency condition alone is one equation in two unknowns; you always need the budget too. Check: plug your bundle back into the budget (it must cost exactly $m$) and compute the MRS there (it must equal $p_1/p_2$).

The tangency gives the maximum when indifference curves are bowed toward the origin (convex preferences) and the solution has positive amounts of both goods. When the tangency would need a negative amount, or the curves are straight or kinked, the best bundle is a corner or a kink: see Corners and Kinks.

blocks.html: Cobb-Douglas utility, $U = x^a y^b$ from Substitutes, Complements, Cobb-Douglas and Quasilinear, is the workhorse of applied economics, because its The Best Affordable Bundle has a short closed form you can remember and check.

With $U = x^a y^b$ (or $a\ln x + b\ln y$), income $m$ and prices $p_1, p_2$: $$x^* = \frac{a}{a + b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_1}, \qquad y^* = \frac{b}{a + b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_2}.$$ The consumer spends the fixed share $a/(a + b)$ of income on $x$ and $b/(a + b)$ on $y$, whatever the prices.

Tangency: $MRS = \dfrac{ay}{bx} = \dfrac{p_1}{p_2}$, so spending on $y$ is $p_2y = \dfrac{b}{a}p_1x$. Put that into the budget: $p_1x + \dfrac{b}{a}p_1x = m$, so $p_1x\cdot\dfrac{a + b}{a} = m$ and $$p_1x^* = \frac{a}{a + b}m.$$ Spending on $x$ is a fixed fraction of income. That is why $x^*$ moves in proportion to income, falls in proportion as $p_1$ rises (own-price elasticity $-1$), and does not depend on $p_2$ at all.

blocks.title: Reading the exponents from spending data
blocks.q: Year after year, Hiro spends 25% of his income on rent and the rest on everything else, even as rents and his income change. If his utility is $U = x^a y^b$ with $a + b = 1$ ($x$ = housing), what is $a$?
steps: Cobb-Douglas says the share of income spent on $x$ is $\dfrac{a}{a + b}$.
With $a + b = 1$ that share is $a$ itself, so $a = 0.25$ and $b = 0.75$.
A constant budget share in the data is the fingerprint of Cobb-Douglas preferences.

blocks.html: Expecting the quantity of $x$ to depend on the price of $y$. With Cobb-Douglas utility it does not: a higher $p_2$ makes $x$ relatively cheaper (pushing $x$ up) but also makes the consumer poorer (pushing $x$ down), and for this utility the two effects cancel exactly. Check: compute spending $p_1x^*$. If it is the same share of income before and after, you have it right.

Real budget shares are not exactly constant (food takes a smaller share of income as people get richer), so Cobb-Douglas is a benchmark, not a law. It is popular because it is easy to solve and often fits well enough for a first estimate.

blocks.html: The tangency rule from The Best Affordable Bundle assumes smooth, bowed indifference curves and some of both goods. Two of the families in Substitutes, Complements, Cobb-Douglas and Quasilinear break those assumptions, and so do budgets too small for a tangency.

Perfect substitutes $U = ax + by$: compare utility per dollar, $a/p_1$ and $b/p_2$, and spend all income on the good with the higher value (any split if they tie). Perfect complements $U = \min\{ax, by\}$: buy at the corner where $ax = by$, so $x^* = \dfrac{m}{p_1 + p_2\,a/b}$.

For substitutes, every dollar on $x$ buys $a/p_1$ units of utility and every dollar on $y$ buys $b/p_2$, no matter how much you already have. So each dollar should go to the better deal, and so should the next one: all of them. The MRS $a/b$ is constant, so it equals $p_1/p_2$ only by coincidence (the tie case). For complements, any unit of $x$ beyond $ax = by$ adds nothing, so money spent on it is wasted; the cheapest way to any utility level is the corner, and the budget picks which corner.

opts.task: Drag the bundle along the budget line. Utility keeps rising all the way to the y-axis.

blocks.cap: $U = x + 2y$ with $p_1 = 3$, $p_2 = 4$: a dollar on $y$ gives $2/4 = 0.5$ util, on $x$ only $1/3$. The best bundle is the corner (0, 15).

blocks.title: Perfect substitutes
steps: $y$ is the better deal at every bundle, so all \$60 goes to $y$: $y = 15$, $x = 0$.
Check against an interior bundle: $(4, 12)$ costs \$60 and gives $4 + 24 = 28$, less than $0 + 30 = 30$.

blocks.title: A quasilinear corner
steps: Tangency would need $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $x = 64$, which costs \$64.
She has only \$20. At every affordable bundle $MRS = 4/\sqrt{x} \ge 4/\sqrt{20} > 1/2$, so she always wants more $x$.
Best bundle: all income on $x$, so $x = 20$, $y = 0$.

blocks.html: Setting the MRS equal to the price ratio for perfect substitutes. For $U = x + 2y$ with $p_1/p_2 = 3/4$, the equation $1/2 = 3/4$ has no solution, and forcing a "mix" gives a bundle that is worse than the corner. Compare utility per dollar instead. Check: whatever bundle you find, compare its utility with the two corners $(m/p_1, 0)$ and $(0, m/p_2)$.

blocks.html: In Lagrange Multipliers you maximized a function along a curve by lining up two gradients. The consumer's problem from The Best Affordable Bundle is exactly that: maximize $U(x, y)$ along the budget line. The method gives the same bundle as substitution, plus one more number with a meaning of its own.

Form $\mathcal{L} = U(x, y) - \lambda(p_1x + p_2y - m)$ and set its three partial derivatives to zero: $$MU_x = \lambda p_1, \qquad MU_y = \lambda p_2, \qquad p_1x + p_2y = m.$$ The multiplier $\lambda = \dfrac{MU_x}{p_1} = \dfrac{MU_y}{p_2}$ is the marginal utility of income: the extra utility from one more dollar.

At the best bundle the indifference curve and the budget line are tangent, so their normal vectors point the same way: $\nabla U = (MU_x, MU_y)$ is parallel to $(p_1, p_2)$, the gradient of the budget. "Parallel" means one is a multiple of the other: $\nabla U = \lambda(p_1, p_2)$. Dividing the first two conditions gives $MU_x/MU_y = p_1/p_2$, the tangency rule. And $\lambda$ is utility per dollar on either good. If income rises by \$1, spending it on either good adds about $\lambda$ to utility, so $dU^*/dm = \lambda$ (this is the envelope theorem).

blocks.name: ec-choice

opts.task: Move income. The optimum slides out along a ray; the tangency condition holds at every income.

blocks.cap: At the optimum (20, 10), $\nabla U$ is perpendicular to the indifference curve and $(p_1, p_2) = (2, 4)$ is perpendicular to the budget line; tangency makes them parallel.

blocks.title: Solving with λ
blocks.q: Maximize $U = xy$ subject to $2x + 4y = 80$.
steps: $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial x = y - 2\lambda = 0$, so $y = 2\lambda$. $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y = x - 4\lambda = 0$, so $x = 4\lambda$.
$x = 20$, $y = 10$. Check the meaning: the maximum utility is $U^* = m^2/32$, so $dU^*/dm = m/16 = 5 = \lambda$.

blocks.title: Log utility
blocks.q: Maximize $U = \ln x + 2\ln y$ subject to $3x + y = 90$. Find $\lambda$.

blocks.html: Solving the first two conditions and stopping. $MU_x = \lambda p_1$ and $MU_y = \lambda p_2$ are two equations in three unknowns $(x, y, \lambda)$: they only tell you the ratio of $x$ to $y$. The third condition, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\lambda = 0$, is the budget itself, and it pins down the scale. Check: your bundle must cost exactly $m$.

The size of $\lambda$ depends on how utility is scaled (double $U$ and $\lambda$ doubles), so compare $\lambda$s only for the same utility function. The same method works with more goods: one condition per good plus the budget. Nothing later in this course needs it; the substitution method always works too.

blocks.html: Turn the consumer's problem around. Instead of "the most utility for income $m$," ask "the least money for utility $\bar u$." This is the problem behind price indexes and money measures of welfare, and it uses the same tangency as Cobb-Douglas Demand and its relatives.

Minimize $p_1x + p_2y$ subject to $U(x, y) = \bar u$. At an interior solution $$MRS = \frac{p_1}{p_2} \quad\text{and}\quad U(x, y) = \bar u.$$ The solution is the compensated (Hicksian) demand $h(p_1, p_2, \bar u)$, and its cost is the expenditure function $E(p_1, p_2, \bar u)$.

Picture a family of parallel budget lines, $p_1x + p_2y = E$, one for each spending level. Start with a large $E$ and slide the line toward the origin. The last line that still touches the target indifference curve touches it at a tangency, where its slope $-p_1/p_2$ equals the curve's slope $-MRS$. Same condition, different constraint. The two problems are linked (duality): if income $m$ buys at most utility $u^*$, then the least money that buys $u^*$ is exactly $m$, and the two problems pick the same bundle.

blocks.name: ec-choice

opts.task: Lower income until the line just touches the curve. That income is the expenditure needed for this utility.

blocks.cap: The target curve $\sqrt{xy} = \sqrt{200}$. At prices (3, 6), \$120 is the least spending that reaches it, at the bundle (20, 10).

blocks.title: Hicksian demand and expenditure
blocks.q: $U = xy$, $p_1 = 4$, $p_2 = 1$. What is the cheapest way to reach $U = 100$?

blocks.title: Duality check
blocks.q: With $U = xy$, $p_1 = 4$, $p_2 = 1$ and income \$40, what utility can the consumer reach? Compare with the example above.
steps: $U^* = 100$, and the least money that reaches 100 was \$40: the two problems give the same bundle.

blocks.html: Three properties of the expenditure function follow from the picture. It rises with $\bar u$ (a higher curve needs a line farther out). It rises with each price, but less than in proportion to one price alone, because the consumer substitutes away from the good that got dearer. And doubling every price exactly doubles $E$, since the cheapest bundle doesn't change. The second fact is why a fixed-basket price index overstates the rise in the cost of living: it prices the old bundle and ignores substitution, which the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics calls substitution bias.

Expecting a different tangency rule when minimizing spending. The condition is still $MRS = p_1/p_2$; what changes is the second equation: the utility target replaces the budget. Check: your answer must sit on the target curve ($U = \bar u$ exactly), and its MRS must equal the price ratio.

Hicksian demand holds utility fixed, so it responds to a price change only through substitution. That makes it the right tool for the Substitution and Income Effects split and for Compensating and Equivalent Variation.

blocks.html: We can't see indifference curves, but we can see choices. If a consumer picks the best bundle in her Budget Sets, as in The Best Affordable Bundle, then every choice tells us something: the chosen bundle beat everything else she could afford.

If bundle A is chosen when bundle B (different from A) was affordable, A is revealed preferred to B. The weak axiom of revealed preference: if A is revealed preferred to B, then B is never chosen when A is affordable.

Suppose she chose A at prices $p$ while B cost no more than A. If her preferences were consistent and she picked her favorite affordable bundle, then $A \succeq B$, and with a strictly bowed indifference map, $A \succ B$. If at other prices she later chose B while A was affordable, the same reasoning gives $B \succ A$. Both can't hold, so a consumer with well-behaved preferences can't produce that pair of choices.

blocks.name: ec-choice

opts.task: Drag the chosen bundles along their lines until the choices are consistent.

blocks.cap: Two budgets with \$40 each. As drawn, each chosen bundle lies inside the other budget, so each was affordable when the other was chosen: a violation. Move the first choice right of the crossing point, or the second one left of it, and the contradiction disappears.

blocks.title: Consistent choices
blocks.q: At prices (2, 4) Sam chose A = (10, 5), spending \$40. At prices (4, 2) he chose B = (4, 12), spending \$40. Check the weak axiom.
steps: At the first prices, B costs $2(4) + 4(12) = 56 > 40$: not affordable, so the first choice says nothing about B.
At the second prices, A costs $4(10) + 2(5) = 50 > 40$: not affordable either.
Neither is revealed preferred to the other: no contradiction.

blocks.title: A violation
blocks.q: At prices (2, 4) Tara chose A = (10, 5), spending \$40. At prices (4, 2) she chose B = (14, 2), spending \$60. Check the weak axiom.
steps: At the first prices, B costs $2(14) + 4(2) = 36 \le 40$: B was affordable, so A is revealed preferred to B.
At the second prices, A costs $4(10) + 2(5) = 50 \le 60$: A was affordable, so B is revealed preferred to A.
Each is revealed preferred to the other, and A and B differ. No consistent preferences that she maximizes could produce both choices.
blocks.a: A violation of the weak axiom.

blocks.html: Checking only whether the two chosen bundles differ, or whether one has more of each good. The test is about affordability: price each chosen bundle at the other situation's prices and compare with what was spent there. Check: write the two costs side by side, "cost of B at prices 1 versus spending 1" and "cost of A at prices 2 versus spending 2." A violation needs both to be affordable.

Revealed preference was introduced by Paul Samuelson in 1938. With many observations, the generalized axiom (Afriat, 1967) tests whether any well-behaved utility function could have produced a whole data set of choices, and it is used to test real spending data.

blocks.html: What Shifts Demand sorted goods into normal and inferior by how demand responds to income. With a utility function we can trace that response exactly: hold prices fixed, raise income, and follow the best bundle from Cobb-Douglas Demand or any other demand.

As income rises the optimum traces the income offer curve; plotting $x$ against income $m$ gives the Engel curve. The income elasticity $$\eta = \frac{dx}{dm}\cdot\frac{m}{x}$$ classifies the good at that income: inferior if $\eta < 0$, normal if $\eta > 0$, a necessity if $0 < \eta < 1$ and a luxury if $\eta > 1$.

Why does 1 separate necessities from luxuries? Look at the budget share $s = px/m$. Differentiate with respect to $m$ (price fixed): $$\frac{ds}{dm} = \frac{p}{m}\frac{dx}{dm} - \frac{px}{m^2} = \frac{px}{m^2}\left(\eta - 1\right).$$ So the share of income spent on the good rises with income exactly when $\eta > 1$ and falls when $\eta < 1$. Food is the classic necessity: richer households spend more on food, but a smaller share of their income (Engel's law, from Ernst Engel's 1857 study of family budgets).

blocks.name: ec-choice

opts.task: Raise income. The optimum moves out along a ray, and the Engel curve below is a straight line through the origin.

blocks.cap: For Cobb-Douglas utility the Engel curve is a ray from the origin, $x = m/(2p_1)$ here, so $\eta = 1$ at every income: the budget share never changes.

blocks.title: A linear Engel curve
blocks.q: Demand for bus rides is $x = 10 + 0.05m$ at fixed prices ($m$ in dollars per month). Find $\eta$ at $m = 200$.
steps: Between 0 and 1: a necessity at this income. A 10% raise brings about 5% more rides.

blocks.title: Normal, then inferior
blocks.q: Demand for store-brand pasta is $x = 8m - 0.1m^2$, with $m$ in thousands of dollars a year. Where does it turn inferior, and what is $\eta$ at $m = 60$?
steps: $\dfrac{dx}{dm} = 8 - 0.2m$, which is zero at $m = 40$. Below 40 thousand dollars the good is normal; above it, inferior.

blocks.html: Treating "inferior" as a fixed label of a good. Whether a good is inferior depends on the person and on where she is on her Engel curve: the pasta above is normal for a low-income household and inferior for a richer one. Check: compute $dx/dm$ at the income in question, not at some other income, and say "inferior at this income."

An income change shifts the budget line in parallel (prices are fixed), so it moves the consumer along her income offer curve. On a market graph it shows up as a shift of the demand curve: right for a normal good, left for an inferior one.

blocks.html: Now hold income fixed and change one price. In Cobb-Douglas Demand the formula $x^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\frac{m}{p_1}$ already told us how $x^*$ responds. Here we see the same thing as a picture, and learn which properties every demand curve has and which it doesn't.

As $p_1$ changes the budget line rotates around its $y$-intercept, and the optimum traces the price offer curve. Plotting $x^*$ against $p_1$ gives the demand curve. Every demand function is homogeneous of degree zero: multiplying all prices and income by the same $k > 0$ leaves the choice unchanged.

Homogeneity: the budget $kp_1x + kp_2y \le km$ is the same set as $p_1x + p_2y \le m$, and preferences didn't change, so the best bundle didn't either. Only relative prices and real income matter, which is why pure inflation (all prices and incomes up together) doesn't change what people buy. Downward slope is not guaranteed by the theory alone. A price fall makes the good relatively cheaper, which always pulls quantity up, and also makes the consumer richer, which pulls quantity up for a normal good but down for an inferior one. Only if that second pull is stronger than the first does demand slope up: a Giffen good.

blocks.name: ec-choice

opts.task: Lower the price of x. Watch the optimum move along the price offer curve and the demand curve fill in.

blocks.cap: With $U = xy$ and \$120, demand is $x^* = 60/p_1$. For Cobb-Douglas the price offer curve is horizontal: spending on $y$, and so $y^*$, doesn't change with $p_1$.

blocks.title: Points on a demand curve
steps: Spending $p_1x^*$ is \$60 every time: a unit-elastic demand curve.

blocks.title: Doubling everything
blocks.q: With $U = xy$, $m = 120$, $p_1 = 3$, $p_2 = 2$, the consumer buys (20, 30). Prices and income all double. What does she buy?
steps: New budget: $6x + 4y = 240$. Divide by 2: $3x + 2y = 120$, the old budget.
Same budget set, same preferences: she still buys (20, 30).

blocks.html: Treating every inferior good as a Giffen good. Inferior means the income effect works against the substitution effect; Giffen means it also wins. Most inferior goods (store brands, bus rides for some people) still have down-sloping demand, because their income effects are small. Check: a Giffen good must be inferior and must take a large share of the budget, so that a price change has a big income effect.

Giffen goods are rare, and for a long time no clean example was known. Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller (2008) found Giffen behavior for rice among very poor households in Hunan, China: when a subsidy made their rice cheaper, some households bought less rice and more of other foods. Economists agree that Giffen goods are possible in theory and unusual in practice.

blocks.html: A price change does two things at once. It changes the trade-off between goods, and it changes how much the consumer can buy overall. Pulling the two apart explains the shapes of the curves in Price Changes and the Demand Curve and Income Changes and Engel Curves, and it uses the compensation idea from Minimizing Spending for a Target Utility.

Split the move from the old optimum A to the new optimum C at a hypothetical B: $$\underbrace{x_C - x_A}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{x_B - x_A}_{\text{substitution effect}} + \underbrace{x_C - x_B}_{\text{income effect}}.$$ B is the choice at the new prices with income adjusted to compensate: Slutsky gives just enough to buy A again, $m' = m + \Delta p_1\,x_A$; Hicks gives just enough to reach A's utility. The substitution effect always moves $x$ against the price change.

Why is the substitution effect never "wrong-way"? Take the Hicks version. B and A sit on the same indifference curve, and B is the cheapest point on it at the new prices, while A was the cheapest at the old prices. If $x$ got cheaper, the cheapest point slides toward more $x$ along a curve bowed toward the origin: the tangency moves to where the curve is flatter, which is at larger $x$. The income effect has no such rule: it is the parallel shift from B to C, and its sign depends on whether the good is normal or inferior. In calculus form this is the Slutsky equation $\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial p_1} = \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial p_1} - x\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial m}$, where $h$ is compensated demand.

blocks.name: ec-slutsky
blocks.cap: $U = xy$, \$120, $p_1$ falling from 4 to 2. A = (15, 60), B = (22.5, 45) on the dashed compensated line, C = (30, 60). Switch to Hicks to keep A's utility instead of A's bundle.

blocks.title: Slutsky decomposition
blocks.q: $U = xy$, $m = 120$, $p_2 = 1$, and $p_1$ falls from 4 to 2. Find the two effects on $x$.
steps: Compensated income: $m' = 120 + (2 - 4)(15) = 90$ (take away what she saves on her old purchases).

blocks.title: Hicks decomposition
blocks.q: $U = xy$, $m = 80$, $p_2 = 1$, $p_1$ falls from 4 to 1.
steps: B: the cheapest bundle with $xy = 400$ at prices (1, 1) has $y = x$, so $x_B = 20$. Substitution effect: $+10$.

blocks.name: ec-slutsky
blocks.cap: An inferior good: the price of $x$ falls, the substitution effect (A to B) adds $x$, and the income effect (B to C) takes some back. For a Giffen good it would take back more than all of it.

blocks.html: Assuming the income effect always works in the same direction as the substitution effect. For a normal good it does; for an inferior good it works against it. Check: ask whether the price change made the consumer richer or poorer, then ask whether this good rises or falls with income. The substitution effect needs no such question: it always goes against the price change.

blocks.html: Price Elasticity of Demand measured elasticity between two points with the midpoint method. With a demand formula and the Constant, Power and Sum Rules, we can measure it at a single point, and we see why it changes along a straight line. In this course elasticity keeps its sign: negative for a demand curve.

$$\varepsilon = \frac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\frac{P}{Q}.$$ For linear demand $Q = a - bP$, $\varepsilon = \dfrac{-bP}{a - bP}$, which runs from 0 to $-\infty$ along the line and equals $-1$ at the midpoint. For constant-elasticity demand $Q = AP^{-k}$, $\varepsilon = -k$ at every price.

Elasticity compares percent changes: $\dfrac{\Delta Q/Q}{\Delta P/P} = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P}\cdot\dfrac{P}{Q}$. As the price step shrinks, $\Delta Q/\Delta P$ becomes the derivative and the midpoint becomes the point itself. Another way to write it: $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\ln Q}{d\ln P}$, the slope on a log–log graph. For $Q = AP^{-k}$, $\ln Q = \ln A - k\ln P$ is a straight line of slope $-k$, which is why that curve has the same elasticity everywhere. That is also why economists often fit log–log regressions: the coefficient on $\ln P$ is an elasticity (see Logs, Dummies and Interactions in Econometrics).

blocks.name: ec-elasticity
blocks.cap: $Q = 100 - 4P$: the slope is the same everywhere, but demand is elastic above $P = 12.5$ and inelastic below it. Revenue peaks where $\varepsilon = -1$.

blocks.title: Linear demand
blocks.q: $Q = 100 - 4P$. Find $\varepsilon$ at $P = 15$.
steps: Elastic: a 1% price rise cuts quantity by about 1.5%, so revenue falls.

blocks.title: Inverse demand
blocks.q: $P = 50 - 2Q$. Find $\varepsilon$ at $Q = 10$.

blocks.title: Constant elasticity
blocks.q: $Q = 500P^{-2}$. Find $\varepsilon$ at $P = 5$ and at $P = 20$.
steps: The same at both prices: a 1% price rise always cuts quantity by about 2%.

blocks.html: Elasticity and revenue are linked by one line of calculus. Revenue is $R = PQ$, so $$\frac{dR}{dP} = Q + P\frac{dQ}{dP} = Q\,(1 + \varepsilon).$$ When demand is elastic ($\varepsilon < -1$) a price rise lowers revenue; when it is inelastic ($-1 < \varepsilon < 0$) a price rise raises revenue; at $\varepsilon = -1$ revenue is at its peak. This is the total revenue test, now with a proof.

Using the slope alone as the elasticity, or using $dP/dQ$ when demand is written as $P$ in terms of $Q$. The slope $-4$ of $Q = 100 - 4P$ is the same everywhere, but the elasticity is $-0.25$ at $P = 5$ and $-3$ at $P = 18.75$. And for $P = 50 - 2Q$ the slope you read off, $-2$, is $dP/dQ$; the formula needs its reciprocal. Check: elasticity has no units. If your answer would change when you measure price in cents instead of dollars, you used a slope, not an elasticity.

blocks.html: Each person's demand curve comes from her own choices, as in Price Changes and the Demand Curve. A market is many buyers facing the same price. To get market demand, add up what all of them want at each price, which produces a piecewise function with kinks.

Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands: $$Q(P) = q_1(P) + q_2(P) + \cdots,$$ where each $q_i(P) = 0$ above that buyer's choke price. Each time the price falls past another buyer's choke price, the market curve gets a kink and becomes flatter.

At a given price every buyer decides alone how much to buy, and the market quantity is the total. So we add quantities at the same price, moving horizontally across the graph. We never add prices: two buyers who each would pay \$5 for a first unit don't make a buyer who would pay \$10. A buyer whose choke price is below the current price buys nothing, not a negative amount, which is why the formula switches when the price crosses a choke price.

blocks.q: With $q_1 = 30 - 2P$ and $q_2 = 24 - 3P$ (each zero when negative), find the market quantity at $P = 10$ and $P = 4$.

blocks.q: Write market demand for the two buyers as a piecewise function.
steps: Check continuity at the kink: $30 - 16 = 14$ and $54 - 40 = 14$.
blocks.a: $Q = 0$, then $30 - 2P$, then $54 - 5P$, with the kink at $P = 8$.

blocks.html: Adding prices instead of quantities, or using $54 - 5P$ at every price. Adding the inverse demands $P = 15 - q/2$ and $P = 8 - q/3$ gives nonsense, because it treats one unit as if both people paid for it. And at $P = 10$ the formula $54 - 5P = 4$ is wrong: it counts buyer 2's "$-6$" units. Check: at any price, find each buyer's quantity first, replace negatives with 0, then add.

Kinks matter beyond the picture. Right at the kink the market's elasticity jumps: just above \$8 only buyer 1 responds to a price change, and just below it both do, so the curve is flatter and more elastic below the kink. A seller who cuts the price past a choke price suddenly reaches a whole new group of buyers.
Public goods are the exception: everyone consumes the same units, so there we add willingness to pay vertically. See Providing Public Goods Efficiently.

blocks.html: Consumer and Producer Surplus measured consumer surplus as a triangle. That works for straight-line demand. For any demand curve the area is an integral, which the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus lets us compute exactly.

With inverse demand $P(q)$, price $p$ and quantity bought $Q$ (where $P(Q) = p$): $$CS = \int_0^Q \big(P(q) - p\big)\,dq = \int_p^{P_{\max}} Q(P)\,dP.$$ When the price falls from $p_0$ to $p_1$, consumer surplus rises by $\Delta CS = \int_{p_1}^{p_0} Q(P)\,dP$.

The height of the demand curve at quantity $q$ is the most someone would pay for the $q$-th unit. Buying it at price $p$ leaves a gain of $P(q) - p$. A thin slice of units of width $dq$ gives a gain of $(P(q) - p)\,dq$, and adding all the slices from the first unit to the last unit bought is the integral. The second formula adds the same area in horizontal slices: at each price level $P$ above $p$, the strip has length $Q(P)$.

blocks.name: ftc
blocks.cap: $P(q) - p$ for demand $P = 20 - 2q$ and price \$8. The area from 0 to $Q = 6$ is consumer surplus, \$36. Past $q = 6$ the integrand is negative: units buyers value at less than the price, which they don't buy.

steps: The demand curve shoots up near $q = 0$, but the area is still finite.

blocks.html: Market consumer surplus is the same integral under the market demand curve, which adds up every buyer's gain. That makes it the standard way to put a dollar value on what buyers gain or lose from a price change, a tax or a new product. It is exact when income effects are small; Compensating and Equivalent Variation shows what changes when they are not.

Integrating the demand curve from 0 to $Q$ without subtracting the price. That gives total willingness to pay: \$84 for the first example, not \$36. Buyers keep only the part above the price; the rectangle $p \times Q = 8 \times 6 = 48$ is what they pay. Check: consumer surplus must be smaller than total willingness to pay by exactly the amount spent.

blocks.html: How much is a price change worth to someone, in dollars? Consumer Surplus as an Integral gives one answer. Two others come straight from utility, using the expenditure function and the income effects from Substitution and Income Effects.

Compensating variation (CV): the income change, after the price change, that brings the person back to her old utility. For a price fall it is the most she would pay to have the change. Equivalent variation (EV): the income change, at the old prices, that would make her as well off as the price change would. With expenditure function $E(p, u)$, for a price fall from $p_0$ to $p_1$: $$CV = m - E(p_1, u_0), \qquad EV = E(p_0, u_1) - m.$$

Both measures ask "how much money is this change like?" but use different reference points. CV holds utility at the old level and prices at the new ones; EV holds utility at the new level and prices at the old ones. When income effects exist, a dollar is worth a different amount of utility at the two reference points, so the answers differ. For a price fall of a normal good, $CV < \Delta CS < EV$. With quasilinear utility there is no income effect on the good, so all three are equal, and Robert Willig (1976) showed that $\Delta CS$ is a close approximation whenever income effects are small.

blocks.cap: With $p_2 = 1$ the vertical axis is money. The price of $x$ falls from \$4 to \$1. CV is the gap between the new budget line and the parallel line tangent to the old curve; EV is the gap between the old line and the parallel line tangent to the new curve.

steps: Demand: $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{x}} = p$, so $x = \dfrac{16}{p^2}$, with no income in it.
With no income effect, extra money all goes to $y$ at a constant marginal utility, so $CV = EV = \Delta CS = 8$.

blocks.html: Assuming CV, EV and the change in consumer surplus are always the same number. They match only without income effects, as with quasilinear utility. In the first example they were \$50, \$69 and \$100. Check: if the good is a big part of the budget and clearly normal (or inferior), expect them to differ, and say which measure a question asks for.

Which measure is "right" depends on the question. CV answers "what would she pay for this change?" (or "what must she be paid to accept it?"). EV answers "what change in income is it equivalent to?" and compares several policies on one scale, because it values everything at the same old prices.

blocks.html: Time is the one thing everyone has the same amount of. Choosing how many hours to work is a consumer choice in disguise: the two "goods" are consumption and leisure, and the tools are the ones from Cobb-Douglas Demand and Substitution and Income Effects.

With $T$ hours, wage $w$ and other income $N$, consumption is $C = w(T - \ell) + N$, or $$C + w\ell = wT + N.$$ Leisure is a good whose price is the wage, and $wT + N$ is full income. Hours worked are $h = T - \ell$. A higher wage has a substitution effect (leisure costs more, so work more) and an income effect (you are richer, so take more leisure). If the income effect wins, labor supply bends backward.

Every hour of leisure costs the $w$ dollars you could have earned, so $w$ is leisure's price. Unlike a price you pay at a store, though, you are a seller of time: when the wage rises, the value of what you own (your $T$ hours) rises too. So a wage rise makes a worker richer, and if leisure is a normal good, that income effect pushes toward more leisure, against the substitution effect. Which effect is bigger is not settled by theory.

opts.task: Raise the wage. Watch leisure and hours worked.

blocks.cap: Leisure across, consumption up. The budget starts at $(24, N)$, with all time as leisure and only other income, and rises with slope $-w$ as leisure is given up for work.

blocks.title: Hours with Cobb-Douglas utility
blocks.q: $U = C\ell$, $T = 24$, $w = 10$, $N = 40$. How many hours does she work?
steps: With $U = C\ell$, half of full income goes to each "good": $w\ell = 140$, so $\ell = 14$.

blocks.title: A raise
blocks.q: Same person, but the wage rises to 20. Then do it again with $N = 0$.
steps: Full income: $20(24) + 40 = 520$, so $\ell = 260/20 = 13$ and $h = 11$. Hours rose.
With $N = 0$: $\ell = \tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{24w}{w} = 12$ at any wage, so $h = 12$ always.
For Cobb-Douglas with no other income, the two effects of a raise cancel exactly. Other income makes the income effect relatively smaller, so hours rise with the wage.
blocks.a: 11 hours with $N = 40$; 12 hours at any wage when $N = 0$.

blocks.title: A backward-bending case
blocks.q: $U = \min\{C, 10\ell\}$ (consumption and leisure in fixed proportion), $T = 16$, $N = 0$. Compare hours at $w = 10$ and $w = 30$.
steps: At the kink $C = 10\ell$, and the budget says $C = w(16 - \ell)$. So $\ell = \dfrac{16w}{w + 10}$.
Fixed proportions leave no room for substitution, so only the income effect acts: a higher wage buys more leisure.
blocks.a: 8 hours, then 4 hours: labor supply bends backward.

blocks.html: Assuming a higher wage always means more hours. That is only the substitution effect. The income effect of a raise pulls toward more leisure, and for some people, at some wages, it wins. Check: decompose the change. If a raise leaves someone richer and leisure is normal, the two effects point in opposite directions, and you need the numbers to know the total.

What the data say: studies generally find that the hours of people who already work respond only modestly to their wage, while the decision whether to work at all responds more. How large these responses are, and how they differ across groups, is still studied and debated, and it matters for questions such as how taxes on earnings affect work.

blocks.html: A dollar today can be invested and become more than a dollar later, so money at different dates can't be added directly. Compound Interest grew money forward. Present value runs the same calculation backward, and Infinite Geometric Series handles payments that go on for many years.

At interest rate $r$ per period: $$PV = \frac{FV}{(1 + r)^t}.$$ An annuity paying $C$ at the end of each of $n$ periods is worth $C\,\dfrac{1 - (1 + r)^{-n}}{r}$; a perpetuity (forever) is worth $\dfrac{C}{r}$; a perpetuity that starts at $C$ and grows at rate $g < r$ is worth $\dfrac{C}{r - g}$.

If you put $PV$ in the bank today, it grows to $PV(1 + r)^t$ in $t$ periods. The present value of $FV$ is the deposit that grows to exactly $FV$, so divide. A stream of payments is worth the sum of each payment's present value. For a perpetuity that is a geometric series with first term $\dfrac{C}{1 + r}$ and ratio $\dfrac{1}{1 + r}$: $$\frac{C/(1 + r)}{1 - 1/(1 + r)} = \frac{C}{r}.$$ An annuity is a perpetuity minus the same perpetuity started $n$ periods later, which gives the factor $1 - (1 + r)^{-n}$.

steps: The formula needs $g < r$; otherwise the payments grow faster than they are discounted and the sum has no finite value.

blocks.html: Multiplying by $(1 + r)^t$ when you should divide, or discounting over the wrong number of periods. Multiplying gives a future value; a present value must be smaller than the amount (for $r > 0$). And a payment at the end of year 1 is discounted once, at the end of year 3 three times. Check: is your present value less than the payment itself? Then count the periods between today and the payment.

blocks.html: Saving and borrowing are choices between consumption now and consumption later. The budget comes from Present Value, and the best choice comes from the tangency in The Best Affordable Bundle.

With income $m_1$ now and $m_2$ later, and interest rate $r$ for both saving and borrowing: $$c_1 + \frac{c_2}{1 + r} = m_1 + \frac{m_2}{1 + r}.$$ The right side is the present value of income. The line passes through the endowment $(m_1, m_2)$ with slope $-(1 + r)$, and at an interior optimum $MRS = 1 + r$.

Saving $s = m_1 - c_1$ (negative for borrowing) earns interest, so $c_2 = m_2 + (1 + r)s$. Substitute $s$ and divide by $1 + r$ to get the budget. Giving up one dollar of $c_1$ buys $1 + r$ dollars of $c_2$, so $1 + r$ is the price of consumption now in units of consumption later. A rise in $r$ rotates the line around the endowment, which is always affordable. For a borrower, a higher rate is bad news on both counts: substitution and income effects both cut $c_1$. For a saver, the substitution effect says "save more," but the higher return makes her richer, and the income effect says "consume more now." Saving can go either way.

steps: Present value of income is 150 either way (no future income to discount).

blocks.html: Thinking a higher interest rate must make every saver save more. The higher return also makes a saver richer, and that income effect raises consumption now. In the example the two effects canceled exactly; with other preferences either can win. Check: ask whether the person is a saver or a borrower first, then sort the two effects.

How much household saving responds to interest rates is an empirical question, and estimates differ. The model's sure lesson is about borrowers and lenders: a higher rate always hurts a borrower and helps a saver.

blocks.html: Many choices are gambles: insurance, investments, a new job. Expected Value averages outcomes in dollars, but people don't treat a sure \$50 like a coin flip for \$0 or \$100. Expected utility averages something else: the utility of each outcome.

A lottery that gives wealth $w_i$ with probability $p_i$ is valued by its expected utility $$E[u(W)] = \sum_i p_i\,u(w_i).$$ Of two lotteries the person prefers the one with the higher expected utility. This is not $u(E[W])$, the utility of the average.

Why not just compare expected values? Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 answer to the St. Petersburg puzzle: a game whose expected payout is infinite is worth only a modest sum to anyone, because an extra dollar means less to a rich person than to a poor one. Weighting utilities instead of dollars captures that. John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern (1944) showed that if preferences over lotteries satisfy a few consistency axioms, they can always be represented this way. Here, unlike in ordinary consumer choice, the scale of $u$ matters: $u$ can be changed only to $a\,u + b$ with $a > 0$.

blocks.name: ec-risk
blocks.cap: $u(W) = \sqrt{W}$, with \$100 three-quarters of the time and \$400 a quarter of the time. The chord between the two outcome points lies below the curve: the expected utility (12.5) is less than the utility of the expected wealth $\sqrt{175} \approx 13.2$.

blocks.title: Expected utility versus expected value
blocks.q: $u(W) = \sqrt{W}$. A lottery pays \$400 with probability 1/4 and \$100 with probability 3/4.

blocks.title: A sure thing or the lottery?
blocks.q: Same person and lottery. Would she trade it for a sure \$150? For a sure \$160?
steps: Even though the lottery's expected value is \$175, she would accept less than that for certainty. The break-even sure amount, $12.5^2 = 156.25$, is her certainty equivalent (next lesson).

blocks.title: Risk can cost more than dollars
blocks.q: With $u = \sqrt{W}$, compare lottery A (equal chances of \$36 and \$196) with lottery B (equal chances of \$81 and \$121).
steps: Expected values: A gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(36 + 196) = 116$; B gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(81 + 121) = 101$.
Expected utilities: A gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(6 + 14) = 10$; B gives $\tfrac{1}{2}(9 + 11) = 10$.
She is indifferent: A's extra \$15 of expected value exactly pays for its much wider spread of outcomes.
blocks.a: Equal expected utility (10), so she is indifferent, though A's expected value is \$15 higher.

blocks.html: Computing the utility of the expected value, $u(E[W])$, instead of the expected utility, $E[u(W)]$. Averaging first throws away the risk: $\sqrt{175}$ treats the lottery as if it paid \$175 for sure. Check: take the utility of each outcome first, then average with the probabilities.

Expected utility is the standard model, and also a debated one. Experiments such as Maurice Allais's (1953) find choices that break its axioms, and alternatives like Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's prospect theory (1979) weight losses and small probabilities differently. Economists broadly use expected utility as the baseline and study where people depart from it.

blocks.html: Expected Utility showed a person who would take a sure \$156.25 instead of a lottery worth \$175 on average. That gap measures how much she dislikes risk, and its source is the shape of $u$, which is about Concavity and the Second Derivative Test.

A person is risk averse when her utility of wealth is concave ($u'' < 0$). Then the certainty equivalent $CE$, the sure wealth with $u(CE) = E[u(W)]$, is below $E[W]$, and the risk premium $E[W] - CE$ is positive. The Arrow-Pratt measure $A(W) = -\dfrac{u''(W)}{u'(W)}$ gauges how risk averse she is at wealth $W$.

For a concave function, the chord between two points of the graph lies below the graph (Jensen's inequality): $$p\,u(w_1) + (1 - p)\,u(w_2) < u(p\,w_1 + (1 - p)\,w_2)$$ The left side is the expected utility, the right side is the utility of the expected wealth. So the sure amount that matches the gamble's expected utility must be less than its expected value. Concavity also means diminishing marginal utility of wealth: the dollars lost in a bad outcome hurt more than the same dollars won in a good outcome help.

blocks.cap: A 50-50 lottery between \$100 and \$400 with $u = \sqrt{W}$: $E[W] = 250$, $E[u] = 15$, $CE = 225$, and the risk premium is \$25. Try the log and linear utilities: with linear utility the risk premium is zero.

blocks.title: Certainty equivalent and risk premium
blocks.q: $u(W) = \sqrt{W}$; wealth is \$400 or \$100 with equal chances.

blocks.title: Log utility
blocks.q: $u(W) = \ln W$; wealth is 64 or 16 (thousand dollars) with equal chances.

blocks.q: With wealth \$100 and $u = \sqrt{W}$, should she accept a coin flip that wins \$44 or loses \$19?
steps: Accept. The expected gain, \$12.50, is more than enough to pay for the risk.

blocks.html: Thinking a risk-averse person refuses every gamble. Risk aversion means she needs to be paid for bearing risk, not that she never bears it: she takes a gamble when its expected gain is large enough to cover her risk premium, as in the last example. Check: compare expected utilities, not "is there risk?"

For $u = \sqrt{W}$, $A(W) = \dfrac{1}{2W}$; for $u = \ln W$, $A(W) = \dfrac{1}{W}$. Both fall as wealth rises, which fits the common observation that richer people take a given dollar gamble more calmly.

blocks.html: Insurance trades a small sure loss (the premium) for protection against a large uncertain one. Risk Aversion and Certainty Equivalents tells us why that can be a good trade even when the premium is more than the expected loss.

A premium is actuarially fair when it equals the expected payout: probability times loss. At a fair price, a risk-averse person buys full coverage. The most she would pay for full coverage is $W - CE$, where $CE$ is the certainty equivalent of going uninsured; the amount above the expected loss she would accept to pay is her risk premium.

Buy $K$ dollars of coverage at $\gamma$ per dollar. Wealth is $W - \gamma K$ with no loss and $W - L + (1 - \gamma)K$ with the loss. Maximize $(1 - \pi)u(W - \gamma K) + \pi\,u(W - L + (1 - \gamma)K)$: $$\pi(1 - \gamma)\,u'(W_{\text{loss}}) = (1 - \pi)\gamma\,u'(W_{\text{no loss}}).$$ At the fair price $\gamma = \pi$ this says $u'(W_{\text{loss}}) = u'(W_{\text{no loss}})$. Because $u'$ falls as wealth rises, the two wealth levels must be equal: full coverage, $K = L$. When $\gamma > \pi$ the buyer keeps part of the risk.

blocks.name: ec-risk
blocks.cap: Wealth \$400 thousand, with a 1/4 chance of losing \$256 thousand. The fair premium for full cover is \$64 thousand. Move the premium: she still buys full coverage up to \$76 thousand.

blocks.title: Fair premium and the most she would pay
blocks.q: Wealth 400 (thousand dollars); a loss of 256 with probability 1/4; $u = \sqrt{W}$.
steps: Full coverage at premium $P$ leaves $400 - P$ for sure. She buys if $400 - P \ge 324$: the most she would pay is 76.
blocks.a: Fair premium 64; she would pay up to 76.

blocks.title: When the price is above fair
blocks.q: Wealth 100 (thousand), loss 50 with probability 0.1, $u = \ln W$, coverage costs 0.15 per dollar. How much coverage does she buy?
steps: The first-order condition with log utility, $$\dfrac{0.1(0.85)}{50 + 0.85K} = \dfrac{0.9(0.15)}{100 - 0.15K}$$ solves to $K = \dfrac{\pi(1 - \gamma)W - (1 - \pi)\gamma(W - L)}{\gamma(1 - \gamma)}$.
Far less than full cover: at an unfair price she insures only part of the loss.

blocks.html: Thinking insurance is a bad buy whenever the premium is above the expected loss. Real insurers must charge more than the expected payout to cover their costs, yet buying can still raise a risk-averse person's expected utility: in the first example she gains from any premium up to 76, well above the expected loss of 64. Check: compare the certain wealth after the premium with the certainty equivalent of staying uninsured.
Insurance also changes behavior and attracts some buyers more than others; Moral Hazard and Incentives and Adverse Selection and Lemons take up those problems.

blocks.html: Short-Run Production counted the extra output from each added worker in a table. A production function $Q = f(K, L)$ says how much output any mix of capital $K$ and labor $L$ can make, and Partial Derivatives turns "the extra output from a little more labor" into an exact rate. The firm side of the course mirrors the consumer side: production functions play the role of utility functions, but their numbers are real output, not just rankings.

$$MP_L = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial L}, \qquad MP_K = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial K}, \qquad AP_L = \frac{Q}{L}.$$ The marginal product is the extra output from a little more of one input, the others held fixed; the average product is output per unit of that input. Diminishing marginal product of labor means $\partial^2 Q/\partial L^2 < 0$.

The marginal product is a slope: hold $K$ fixed, and $Q$ becomes a function of $L$ alone, whose derivative is $MP_L$. The average product is a different number, and the two are linked: $$\frac{d}{dL}\left(\frac{Q}{L}\right) = \frac{L\cdot MP_L - Q}{L^2} = \frac{MP_L - AP_L}{L}.$$ So the average rises while the marginal worker adds more than the average and falls once she adds less, the same way a new test score pulls your average up only if it beats your average.

In the first example the average is 20 while the next worker adds only 10, and a firm deciding whether to hire needs the 10. blocks.html: The level curves of a production function play the role that indifference curves played for the consumer. Building on Production Functions and Marginal Products and the logic of The Marginal Rate of Substitution, the slope of a level curve says how one input can replace another.

An isoquant is every combination of inputs that makes the same output, $f(K, L) = q$. With labor across and capital up, the size of its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution $$MRTS = \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = -\frac{dK}{dL}\Big|_{Q \text{ fixed}},$$ the capital that one more worker can replace with output unchanged. For $Q = AK^\alpha L^\beta$, $MRTS = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}\cdot\dfrac{K}{L}$.

Along $f(K, L) = q$, differentiate with respect to $L$: $MP_K\dfrac{dK}{dL} + MP_L = 0$. So $\dfrac{dK}{dL} = -\dfrac{MP_L}{MP_K}$. In words: removing $\Delta K$ machines loses about $MP_K\,\Delta K$ units; adding $\Delta L$ workers gains about $MP_L\,\Delta L$; output stays put when they match. With diminishing marginal products, each extra worker replaces less capital, so isoquants bow toward the origin.

blocks.cap: Isoquants of $Q = \sqrt{KL}$. At (L, K) = (4, 16), $MRTS = K/L = 4$: one more worker can replace about 4 machines. At (16, 4) it is only $1/4$.

$Q = \min\{K, L/2\}$: each unit needs one machine and two workers. Isoquants are L-shaped, with corners where $L = 2K$; extra of one input alone adds nothing.

blocks.html: Flipping the ratio to $MP_K/MP_L$, or reading an isoquant as a set of input mixes with equal cost. With labor on the horizontal axis, labor's marginal product goes on top. And an isoquant holds output fixed; the lines of equal cost are isocost lines, which depend on input prices and come in Cost Minimization. Check: at a bundle with lots of capital and few workers, a worker should be able to replace a lot of capital, so the MRTS should be large.

blocks.html: What happens if a firm doubles everything: twice the workers, twice the machines, twice the floor space? The answer is a property of the production function, and it is what shapes the long-run cost curve in Economies and Diseconomies of Scale.

Multiply every input by $t > 1$. If output rises by more than $t$, the technology has increasing returns to scale; by exactly $t$, constant; by less, decreasing. For $Q = AK^\alpha L^\beta$: $$f(tK, tL) = t^{\alpha + \beta}f(K, L),$$ so returns are increasing, constant or decreasing as $\alpha + \beta$ is greater than, equal to or less than 1.

$A(tK)^\alpha(tL)^\beta = t^\alpha t^\beta AK^\alpha L^\beta$. The exponents add because both inputs are scaled together. Returns to scale and diminishing marginal product answer different questions. Diminishing $MP_L$ asks what happens when labor alone grows, with the building and machines fixed: workers crowd each other. Returns to scale asks what happens when all inputs grow together: the firm builds a second plant as well as hiring. A technology can have both diminishing marginal products and constant returns.

blocks.html: Concluding that diminishing marginal products mean decreasing returns to scale. The second example has diminishing marginal products and constant returns. Check: to test returns to scale, scale every input by the same factor and compare output with that factor. Never test it by changing one input.

Returns to scale drive long-run costs. With constant returns and fixed input prices, doubling output doubles cost, so long-run average cost is flat; increasing returns give economies of scale (falling average cost); decreasing returns give diseconomies.

blocks.html: A firm that wants to make $q$ units should make them as cheaply as possible. The Least-Cost Mix of Inputs said "spend so the last dollar on each input buys the same output." With isoquants and Optimization we can find the exact mix.

Minimize $wL + rK$ subject to $f(K, L) = q$. At an interior solution $$MRTS = \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = \frac{w}{r}, \quad\text{equivalently}\quad \frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r},$$ together with the isoquant $f(K, L) = q$.

An isocost line $wL + rK = C$ shows every mix costing $C$; its slope is $-w/r$. Slide isocost lines toward the origin until the last one still touches the isoquant: there they are tangent, so the isoquant's slope $-MRTS$ equals $-w/r$. In per-dollar terms: if $MP_L/w > MP_K/r$, moving a dollar from capital to labor adds output, so the firm could cut cost and keep output the same. Only equal output per dollar leaves nothing to gain. This is the producer's version of the consumer's tangency in Minimizing Spending for a Target Utility.

blocks.html: The same tangency can be found with a Lagrange multiplier: minimize $wL + rK - \mu\,(f(K, L) - q)$. The conditions $w = \mu MP_L$ and $r = \mu MP_K$ give $MP_L/MP_K = w/r$, and the multiplier $\mu$ turns out to be marginal cost: the extra cost of one more unit of output.

Setting the MRTS equal to $r/w$, or spending everything on whichever input has the lower price. The tangency compares labor's marginal product per dollar with capital's, so the wage goes with labor: $MP_L/w = MP_K/r$, or $MRTS = w/r$. And a cheap input is not a bargain if it adds little output; what matters is output per dollar. Check: if labor gets dearer, your answer should use relatively more capital.

blocks.html: Solving Cost Minimization for every output gives the cost function: the least cost of producing each $q$. From it come the cost measures of Short-Run Costs, now with the Constant, Power and Sum Rules doing the work.
$C(q)$ is the least cost of producing $q$. In the short run $C(q) = F + VC(q)$, with fixed cost $F = C(0)$. Then $$MC(q) = C'(q), \qquad AC(q) = \frac{C(q)}{q}, \qquad AVC(q) = \frac{VC(q)}{q}.$$

Marginal cost is the extra cost of a little more output: the slope of total cost, $\lim \Delta C/\Delta q$. Fixed cost doesn't change with $q$, so its derivative is zero: a rent, a license fee or a lump-sum tax moves $AC$ but leaves $MC$ alone. Where the cost function comes from production: with $Q = \sqrt{KL}$ and capital fixed at $\bar K$, making $q$ needs $L = q^2/\bar K$, so $$C(q) = r\bar K + \frac{w}{\bar K}q^2, \qquad MC(q) = \frac{2w}{\bar K}q.$$ Marginal cost rises because labor's marginal product falls.

items: $MC$ decides how much to produce: compare it with price or marginal revenue.
$AVC$ decides whether to produce at all in the short run (the shutdown rule).
$AC$ decides whether the firm earns a profit, and whether firms enter or leave in the long run.

blocks.html: Differentiating average cost to get marginal cost, or letting fixed cost appear in marginal cost. $MC$ is the derivative of total cost; the derivative of $AC$ tells you where $AC$ is rising or falling, which is a different question (see Where Average Cost Is Lowest). blocks.html: In the short run some inputs, usually the plant and its machines, are fixed. In the long run everything can change. Comparing the two cost functions explains the shape of the long-run average cost curve.

For any output, short-run cost with capital fixed at $\bar K$ is never below long-run cost: $$C_{SR}(q; \bar K) \ge C_{LR}(q),$$ with equality at the output for which $\bar K$ is the best plant. The long-run average cost curve is the lower envelope of the short-run average cost curves: it touches each one at a single point.

The long run chooses the cheapest of all input mixes, including the one with capital $\bar K$. A minimum over a bigger set can't be higher than the minimum over a smaller set, so $C_{LR} \le C_{SR}$. They are equal when $\bar K$ is exactly the capital the long run would pick. Away from that output, the fixed plant is the wrong size: too small (workers crowd the machines) or too big (machines sit idle).

blocks.cap: Short-run average cost curves for several plant sizes and the long-run curve hugging them from below. Each short-run curve touches the long-run curve at one output, which is usually not that short-run curve's own minimum.

steps: Long run: $K/L = w/r = 1$, so $K = L = q$ and $C_{LR} = 2q$.
$q = 10$: both cost 20. $q = 20$: short run $10 + 40 = 50$, long run 40.
blocks.a: Equal (20) at $q = 10$; at $q = 20$ the short run costs \$10 more.

blocks.title: Where they touch

blocks.html: Thinking the long-run average cost curve passes through the lowest point of every short-run curve. It touches each short-run curve where that plant is the best choice for the output. When long-run average cost is falling, the touching point is to the left of the short-run minimum (it pays to run a slightly bigger plant below its best output); when it is rising, to the right. Only at the bottom of the long-run curve do the two minimums coincide. Check: compare slopes at the touching point. Both curves have the same slope there, so if the long-run curve is falling, so is the short-run one.

With constant returns to scale and fixed input prices, as in these examples, long-run average cost is flat ($C_{LR}/q = 2\sqrt{wr}$), and each short-run curve touches it exactly at its own minimum. The envelope shape with economies and diseconomies of scale comes from returns to scale that change with size.

blocks.html: In Cost Functions and Marginal Cost you saw marginal cost cross average cost at the bottom of the average cost curve. The The Quotient Rule shows that this is not a coincidence of the pictures but a fact about every cost function.
$$AC'(q) = \frac{MC(q) - AC(q)}{q}.$$ So average cost falls while $MC < AC$, rises while $MC > AC$, and is lowest where $MC = AC$. The same holds for average variable cost and $MC$.

By the quotient rule, $$\frac{d}{dq}\left(\frac{C(q)}{q}\right) = \frac{qC'(q) - C(q)}{q^2} = \frac{C'(q) - C(q)/q}{q}.$$ The intuition is the grade-point average: one more unit costing more than the current average pulls the average up, and one costing less pulls it down. At the bottom the marginal unit costs exactly the average. Setting $MC = 0$ finds where total cost is flat, which is a different (and usually meaningless) point.

Setting marginal cost equal to zero to find the lowest average cost. For $C = 100 + q^2$, $MC = 2q = 0$ gives $q = 0$, where average cost is infinite. The minimum of a ratio comes from the derivative of the ratio: set $MC = AC$. Check: at your answer, compute both MC and AC. They must be equal.

blocks.html: A competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it likes at the market price $p$, and nothing above it. The Shutdown Rule told it when to stay open; with a cost function and Where Average Cost Is Lowest we can derive its whole supply curve.

A price taker maximizes $\pi(q) = pq - C(q)$. It produces where $$p = MC(q)$$ on the rising part of marginal cost, as long as $p$ is at least the minimum of average variable cost. Below that price it produces nothing. Its short-run supply curve is the part of $MC$ above minimum $AVC$.

First-order condition: $\pi'(q) = p - C'(q) = 0$. Second-order condition: $\pi''(q) = -C''(q) < 0$, so marginal cost must be rising; where MC is falling, $p = MC$ marks a profit minimum. Then compare with shutting down: producing gives $pq - VC(q) - F$, shutting down gives $-F$ (the fixed cost is owed either way in the short run). Producing is better exactly when $pq \ge VC(q)$, that is, $p \ge AVC(q)$.

Each firm's curve starts at its own shutdown price, so the market curve has a step or kink wherever a group of firms enters.

Taking the whole MC curve as the supply curve. The falling part of MC is where $p = MC$ gives a profit minimum, and the part below minimum AVC is where the firm would rather shut down. Check: at your quantity, MC must be rising and the price must be at least AVC.

blocks.html: The seller's side of surplus mirrors Consumer Surplus as an Integral. A competitive firm sells each unit at the price $p$, and the unit costs it $MC(q)$ to make. Adding the gaps is an integral, evaluated with Evaluating Integrals with FTC Part 2.

$$PS = \int_0^q \big(p - MC(x)\big)\,dx = pq - VC(q) = \pi + F.$$ Producer surplus is revenue minus variable cost. It equals profit plus the fixed cost, so it is larger than profit whenever there is a fixed cost.

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $\int_0^q MC(x)\,dx = C(q) - C(0) = VC(q)$: adding up marginal costs gives back variable cost, and the fixed cost (which is $C(0)$) never shows up. So $PS = pq - VC(q)$. Profit subtracts the fixed cost as well. In the short run the fixed cost is owed whether or not the firm produces, so producer surplus measures what the firm gains from producing rather than shutting down. For a market, the same integral under the market supply curve adds up every firm's surplus.

blocks.title: A market

blocks.html: Why use producer surplus rather than profit to judge a policy? Because the fixed cost is the same whether a tax, a price control or a new competitor comes along, so it cancels out of every comparison. The change in producer surplus equals the change in profit, and it is what the area above the supply curve measures. In the long run, when nothing is fixed, producer surplus is the return to whatever is scarce: the best land, a good location, a rare skill.

Treating producer surplus as profit. They differ by the fixed cost: in the first example, \$100 versus \$50. Check: if your producer surplus changes when you change only the fixed cost, you have computed profit instead.

blocks.html: In the short run the number of firms is fixed. In the long run firms can enter when there is profit to be made and leave when there are losses, as in Entry, Exit and the Long Run. With identical firms and the supply rule, we can solve for everything.

With free entry and exit and identical firms, the long-run price equals the minimum of long-run average cost: $$p^* = \min_q AC(q).$$ Each firm produces $q^*$, the output at that minimum, and the number of firms is $n = Q_D(p^*)/q^*$.

If the price were above minimum average cost, a new firm could produce $q^*$ and earn a positive economic profit, so firms enter. Entry shifts market supply right and pushes the price down. If the price were below minimum average cost, every firm would lose money and some would leave, pushing the price up. Only at $p^* = AC_{\min}$ is there no reason to enter or exit. At that price each firm sets $p^* = MC$, and $MC = AC$ at the bottom of AC, so each firm produces $q^*$ and earns zero economic profit: a normal return on everything it owns.

blocks.html: Letting the price stay above minimum average cost in the long run, or counting firms with the short-run output per firm. A price above $AC_{\min}$ means profits that attract entry; the count of firms must use $q^*$ at the bottom of AC, not the larger quantity each firm produces when the price is temporarily high. Check: in long-run equilibrium every firm's profit is zero and $p = MC = AC$.

If the industry's growth bids up the price of an input it uses heavily (land, specialized labor), each firm's costs rise as the industry expands, and the long-run supply curve slopes up (an increasing-cost industry). The zero-profit logic still holds at each point.
