blocks.html: Who Really Pays a Tax showed that the side of the market that responds less to price bears more of a tax, whoever pays it legally. With Point Elasticity with Calculus we can say exactly how much.

For a small per-unit tax $t$, the price buyers pay rises by $$\Delta P_b = \frac{\varepsilon_S}{\varepsilon_S + |\varepsilon_D|}\,t,$$ and the price sellers keep falls by $\Delta P_s = \dfrac{|\varepsilon_D|}{\varepsilon_S + |\varepsilon_D|}\,t$. The less elastic side bears the larger share. It doesn't matter which side sends the money to the government.

Start at equilibrium $(P, Q)$. After the tax, buyers pay $P + \Delta P_b$ and sellers keep $P - \Delta P_s$, with $\Delta P_b + \Delta P_s = t$. Quantity demanded falls by about $|\varepsilon_D|\,Q\,\dfrac{\Delta P_b}{P}$; quantity supplied falls by about $\varepsilon_S\,Q\,\dfrac{\Delta P_s}{P}$. The market still clears, so the two falls are equal: $|\varepsilon_D|\,\Delta P_b = \varepsilon_S\,\Delta P_s$. Solving with $\Delta P_b + \Delta P_s = t$ gives the formula. Notice the "other side's" elasticity on top: buyers bear more when supply is very elastic, because sellers can easily walk away.

blocks.q: $Q_d = 100 - 2P$, $Q_s = 3P - 20$, and a tax of \$5 per unit on sellers.
steps: Buyers' share: $3/5 = 0.6$. Elasticity check at (24, 52): $\varepsilon_D = -\tfrac{12}{13}$, $\varepsilon_S = \tfrac{18}{13}$, and $\dfrac{18/13}{18/13 + 12/13} = 0.6$.

blocks.html: Giving the larger share to the more elastic side, which turns the formula upside down. The side that can easily change how much it buys or sells escapes the tax; the side that can't, pays. Check: if demand were perfectly inelastic ($\varepsilon_D = 0$), your formula should give buyers the whole tax: $\varepsilon_S/(\varepsilon_S + 0) = 1$.

For straight-line curves the result is exact for any tax size: buyers bear $d/(b + d)$ when $Q_d = a - bP$ and $Q_s = c + dP$. For curved demand and supply it holds for small taxes, using the elasticities at the starting point.

blocks.html: A tax raises revenue, but it also stops some trades that would have helped both sides. The value lost on those trades is the deadweight loss. With Tax Incidence with Elasticities and the surplus integrals of Consumer Surplus as an Integral and Producer Surplus as an Integral, we can measure it and see how it grows with the tax.

The deadweight loss of a per-unit tax is the value of the lost trades: $$DWL = \int_{Q_t}^{Q^*}\big(P_D(Q) - P_S(Q)\big)\,dQ \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,t\,\Delta Q.$$ With straight lines, $\Delta Q = \dfrac{bd}{b + d}\,t$, so $DWL = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{bd}{b + d}\,t^2$: it grows with the square of the tax.

Each unit between $Q_t$ and $Q^*$ was worth $P_D(Q)$ to some buyer and cost only $P_S(Q)$ to make, so it would have added $P_D - P_S$ to total surplus. The tax prevents it. The gap is $t$ at $Q_t$ (that is what the tax wedge means) and 0 at $Q^*$, so with straight lines the lost area is a triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2}t\,\Delta Q$. Doubling the tax doubles both the height and the base: four times the area. In elasticity form (the Harberger approximation), $DWL \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\,t^2\,\dfrac{Q}{P}\cdot\dfrac{\varepsilon_S|\varepsilon_D|}{\varepsilon_S + |\varepsilon_D|}$: taxes on goods with very inelastic demand or supply waste less.

A practical consequence that economists broadly agree on: raising a given amount of revenue with a low rate on a broad base wastes less than a high rate on a narrow base, other things equal. Which taxes are fair, and how to weigh efficiency against fairness, are separate questions on which people disagree.

blocks.html: The Monopolist's Price and Output found a monopoly's output where MR = MC and read its price off the demand curve. With a cost function, an inverse demand $p(q)$ and the The Product Rule, the same rule falls out of one derivative.

A single-price monopoly maximizes $\pi(q) = p(q)\,q - C(q)$. The first-order condition is $$MR(q) = p(q) + q\,p'(q) = MC(q).$$ Because $p'(q) < 0$, marginal revenue is below price. The price is then read from the demand curve at that $q$.

Revenue is a product, $R(q) = p(q)\cdot q$. The product rule splits its derivative into two pieces. Selling one more unit brings in its price, $p(q)$: the gain. But to sell it the firm must lower the price on all $q$ units it was already selling, by $p'(q)$ each: the loss, $q\,p'(q)$. A competitive firm has $p' = 0$, so for it $MR = p$; a monopoly does not. For linear demand $p = a - bq$, $MR = a - 2bq$: the same intercept and twice the slope.

blocks.html: Two checks finish the problem. Second-order: profit must curve down at your $q$, which holds when $MR$ falls faster than $MC$. And shutdown: compare the profit at your $q$ with what the firm gets from producing nothing. One more consequence: a monopoly has no supply curve. Its output depends on the whole shape of demand (through MR), not on the price alone, so two different demand curves can lead it to the same price with different quantities.

In the first example $p = MC$ would give $q = 40$ and a price of 20, which leaves the monopoly's profit at minus the fixed cost. And $\dfrac{d}{dq}[p(q)\,q]$ needs the product rule: $p(q) + q\,p'(q)$. Check: your MR must be below the demand curve at every $q > 0$, and your price must come from the demand curve, not from MR or MC.

blocks.html: How high is a monopoly's price above its marginal cost? Combine Monopoly with Calculus with Point Elasticity with Calculus and the answer depends on one number: how elastic demand is at the chosen price.

At the profit-maximizing price, $$L = \frac{p - MC}{p} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|}.$$ $L$ is the Lerner index, the markup as a share of price. The less elastic demand is, the bigger the markup. A firm with positive marginal cost never chooses a price where demand is inelastic ($|\varepsilon| < 1$).

Rewrite marginal revenue with the elasticity: $$MR = p + q\,\frac{dp}{dq} = p\left(1 + \frac{q}{p}\frac{dp}{dq}\right) = p\left(1 + \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right) = p\left(1 - \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|}\right).$$ Set $MR = MC$: $p - MC = p/|\varepsilon|$, which is the rule. If $|\varepsilon| < 1$, MR is negative: cutting output a little would raise revenue and save cost, so that can't be the best choice. With $MC > 0$ the optimum needs $MR > 0$, so $|\varepsilon| > 1$.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: $p = 100 - 2q$, MC = 20: the monopoly sells 20 units at \$60. There $|\varepsilon| = 1.5$ and the markup is $40/60 = 2/3 = 1/1.5$. The optimum is on the upper, elastic half of the demand line.

blocks.title: Price from the markup rule
blocks.q: At its optimum a firm faces $\varepsilon = -3$, and its marginal cost is \$20. What price does it charge?

blocks.title: Elasticity from prices
blocks.q: A profit-maximizing firm charges \$50 with marginal cost \$30. What is the elasticity of demand at that price?

blocks.title: Checking with a linear demand
blocks.q: For $p = 100 - 2q$ and $MC = 20$, the optimum is $q = 20$, $p = 60$. Verify the rule.

blocks.html: For constant-elasticity demand $q = Ap^{-k}$, the rule gives the price directly: $p = MC\cdot\dfrac{k}{k - 1}$. With $k = 2$ the price is twice marginal cost; with $k = 5$ it is 25% above; as $k$ grows the markup shrinks toward zero, the competitive limit.

Thinking a firm with market power picks a price where demand is inelastic, because "buyers can't do without it." If demand were inelastic at its price, a price rise would raise revenue while cutting the quantity it must produce: more revenue, less cost. It would keep raising the price until demand became elastic. Check: compute $|\varepsilon|$ at the claimed optimum. With $MC > 0$ it must exceed 1.

The Lerner index is a common measure of market power, with a caution: in industries with large fixed costs (software, medicines), prices well above marginal cost can go with zero economic profit, because the markup pays for the fixed cost. A high markup alone does not prove high profit.

blocks.html: Price Discrimination showed a seller charging different groups different prices. If the seller can tell the groups apart and stop resale between them, the markup rule tells it exactly what to charge each one.

With one marginal cost and separate markets, set $$MR_1(q_1) = MR_2(q_2) = MC.$$ Each market's price follows the markup rule $p_i\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{|\varepsilon_i|}\right) = MC$, so the market with the less elastic demand pays the higher price.

Suppose $MR_1 > MR_2$. Selling one unit fewer in market 2 and one more in market 1 leaves cost unchanged and raises revenue by $MR_1 - MR_2$. So at the optimum the marginal revenues must be equal, and each must equal MC (otherwise changing total output pays). Equal MRs do not mean equal prices: a market where buyers are less sensitive to price gets a bigger markup.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Two markets with MC = 10: students ($p = 40 - q$) and other adults ($p = 80 - 2q$). MR = MC in each gives prices \$25 and \$45.

blocks.title: Two linear markets
blocks.q: Students: $p_1 = 40 - q_1$. Other adults: $p_2 = 80 - 2q_2$. $MC = 10$, no resale.
steps: Elasticities at those points: students $\dfrac{25}{15} \approx 1.67$, adults $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{45}{17.5} \approx 1.29$. The adults' demand is less elastic, and they pay more.

blocks.title: Constant elasticities
blocks.q: MC = \$6. Market A has $\varepsilon = -2$ and market B has $\varepsilon = -4$.

blocks.html: Setting the prices, rather than the marginal revenues, equal across markets, or charging more where demand is more elastic. Equal prices throw away the profit from tailoring each price; a high price where buyers are very price-sensitive drives them away. Check: compute MR in each market at your quantities. They must be equal to each other and to MC.

Three conditions make this possible: market power, a way to tell groups apart (age, location, time of purchase), and no resale. Whether discrimination raises or lowers total surplus compared with one price depends on the case: it can open a market that a single price would leave unserved, or it can cut total output.

blocks.html: A gym charges a membership fee plus a price per class; an amusement park charges admission plus a price per ride. With identical customers, Monopoly with Calculus and Consumer Surplus as an Integral show how to set both parts.

With identical customers, the profit-maximizing two-part tariff sets the per-unit price equal to marginal cost and the entry fee equal to each customer's consumer surplus at that price. The firm captures the whole surplus, and output is efficient.

Profit from one customer at unit price $p$ is the per-unit margin plus the largest fee she will pay, her consumer surplus: $$\pi(p) = (p - c)\,q(p) + CS(p).$$ Since $CS'(p) = -q(p)$ (raising the price removes a strip of surplus as wide as the quantity), $$\pi'(p) = q(p) + (p - c)\,q'(p) - q(p) = (p - c)\,q'(p),$$ which is zero at $p = c$. Any price above cost shrinks the surplus that the fee collects by more than it adds in margin; the difference is the deadweight-loss triangle.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: One customer with $p = 20 - q$ and MC = 4. At a per-unit price of 4 she buys 16 units, and the fee takes her whole surplus, \$128.

blocks.title: Setting the tariff
blocks.q: Each customer has $p = 20 - q$; MC is \$4.
steps: Per-unit price $= 4$, so each customer buys $q = 16$.

blocks.title: Compared with a single price
blocks.q: Same customers, but only one price per unit and no fee.
steps: The two-part tariff earns twice as much: it takes the whole triangle of surplus, where the single price gets a rectangle half its size and leaves a deadweight loss.

blocks.html: The two-part tariff is efficient: every unit worth more than its cost to a customer gets made, so there is no deadweight loss. What changes is who keeps the surplus. Under competition the customers would keep the \$128 per head; here the firm takes it all through the fee. With 500 customers, profit is $500 \times 128 = \$64{,}000$.

Keeping the monopoly per-unit price and adding a fee. At $p = 12$ the customer's surplus is only $\tfrac{1}{2}(8)(8) = 32$, so the most profit is $64 + 32 = 96$, less than 128. Check: compare total profit (margin plus fee) at your price with profit at $p = MC$.

With customers who differ, the answer changes: a fee high enough to take a big user's surplus drives out small users, so the best tariff usually sets the per-unit price somewhat above marginal cost and the fee at the smallest customers' surplus. The identical-customer case shows the core logic.

blocks.html: Monopsony described a single big employer that must raise pay for everyone to attract one more worker. With an upward-sloping supply curve $w(L)$, a marginal revenue product from Production Functions and Marginal Products, and the The Product Rule, we can find its hiring and its wage.

A monopsony employer pays $w(L)$ to each of $L$ workers, so its wage bill is $w(L)\,L$ and the marginal cost of labor is $$MCL = w(L) + L\,w'(L) > w(L).$$ It hires where $MRP = MCL$ and pays the wage on the supply curve at that $L$.

The product rule splits the cost of one more worker in two: her own wage, $w(L)$, and the raise everyone else gets, $L\,w'(L)$. Hiring stops where the value of one more worker's output (MRP) equals that full cost. But the wage itself is whatever the supply curve says is needed to attract $L$ workers, which is less than MCL. The result is fewer workers and a lower wage than in a competitive labor market, where hiring would continue until $MRP = w(L)$.

blocks.name: ec-factor

opts.task: Turn on the minimum wage and move it between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage.

blocks.cap: Supply $w = 7 + 2L$, $MCL = 7 + 4L$, $MRP = 67 - L$. The monopsony hires 12 at \$31; a competitive market would reach 20 at \$47.

blocks.title: Hiring and the wage
blocks.q: $w(L) = 7 + 2L$ and $MRP = 67 - L$.
steps: Wage from the supply curve: $7 + 24 = 31$. (MRP there is 55; MCL is 55 too.)

blocks.title: A minimum wage in the model
blocks.q: Same employer, with a minimum wage of \$40.
steps: Up to the point where the supply curve reaches \$40 ($7 + 2L = 40$, so $L = 16.5$), every worker costs exactly \$40, so $MCL = 40$ there.
$MRP = 67 - L$ is above 40 until $L = 27$, so the employer hires all 16.5 workers willing to work at \$40.
Employment rises from 12 to 16.5 and the wage from \$31 to \$40.

blocks.html: Reading the wage off the marginal cost of labor at the chosen $L$. MCL at $L = 12$ is \$55, but no one is paid that: the employer pays the lowest wage that attracts 12 workers, \$31, from the supply curve. Check: the wage you report must satisfy $w = w(L)$ for the $L$ you found.

What economists broadly agree on and what they debate: in the competitive model a binding minimum wage reduces employment; in the monopsony model a moderate one can raise it, as above. Which model better describes a given labor market, and the measured employment effects of particular minimum wages, are studied and debated.

blocks.html: Nash Equilibrium and the Prisoner's Dilemma introduced the prisoner's dilemma, where each player has one obvious choice. Most games are less tidy: what is best for you depends on what the other player does. The tool for any game in a matrix is the best response.

A best response is a player's best choice given what the other player does. A Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices that are best responses to each other: no player can gain by changing alone. To find all pure-strategy equilibria, mark each player's best responses; every cell with both payoffs marked is an equilibrium. A game can have none, one, or several.

Underlining checks the definition cell by cell. For the row player, go column by column and underline the largest first number: that is her best reply to that column. For the column player, go row by row and underline the largest second number. A cell with both underlined is one where neither player could do better by switching alone, which is exactly what equilibrium means. Nothing in the definition says the result is good for the players, or unique.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: A coordination game: both players gain from choosing the same option. Both (A, A) and (B, B) are equilibria; once either is reached, no one wants to switch alone.

blocks.title: Two equilibria
blocks.q: Two firms pick a charging-plug standard. Payoffs (Firm 1, Firm 2): both pick A: (3, 3); both pick B: (2, 2); they differ: (0, 0). Find all pure-strategy equilibria.
steps: If Firm 2 picks A, Firm 1's best response is A (3 > 0); if Firm 2 picks B, it is B (2 > 0).
(A, A) and (B, B) both have both payoffs underlined. (A, A) is better for both, but (B, B) is still an equilibrium: once there, neither gains by switching alone.

blocks.title: A three-by-three game
blocks.q: Row picks Top, Middle or Bottom; Column picks Left, Center or Right. Payoffs: Top (4, 4), (3, 2), (4, 5); Middle (9, 7), (6, 1), (5, 0); Bottom (8, 7), (8, 6), (8, 0).
steps: Row's best responses: vs Left, Middle (9); vs Center, Bottom (8); vs Right, Bottom (8).
Column's best responses: vs Top, Right (5); vs Middle, Left (7); vs Bottom, Left (7).

blocks.html: Stopping after finding one equilibrium. Coordination games, like the plug standard, have two or more, and which one people reach depends on history, expectations or a focal point. Check every cell before you stop: the count matters, because a game with several equilibria needs something outside the matrix to predict what happens.

blocks.html: Some games have no pure-strategy equilibrium: in matching pennies, whatever one player does, the other wants to switch. With Best Responses and Nash Equilibrium and Expected Value, we can find the equilibrium that always exists: players randomize.

In a mixed-strategy equilibrium each player randomizes so that the other player is indifferent between her choices. So each player's probabilities are found from the other player's payoffs. John Nash proved in 1950 that every game with finitely many players and choices has at least one equilibrium, possibly in mixed strategies.

Suppose Row mixes between Up and Down. That only makes sense if Up and Down give her the same expected payoff; if one were better, she would play it for sure. Her expected payoffs depend on Column's mix $q$, not her own. So Column's $q$ must be the one that makes Row indifferent, and by the same reasoning Row's $p$ must make Column indifferent. A useful consequence: changing Row's own payoffs changes Column's equilibrium mix, not Row's.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: Matching pennies. Move each player's mixing probability. The other player's two expected-payoff lines cross where she is indifferent, at 1/2.

blocks.title: An asymmetric game
blocks.q: Payoffs (Row, Column): Up–Left (3, 3), Up–Right (6, 4), Down–Left (2, 11), Down–Right (9, 6). Find the mixed equilibrium.
steps: No pure equilibrium: Row prefers Up against Left and Down against Right; Column prefers Right against Up and Left against Down.
Row's $p$ (Up) makes Column indifferent: Left gives $3p + 11(1 - p)$, Right gives $4p + 6(1 - p)$. Equal when $11 - 8p = 6 - 2p$, so $p = 5/6$.
Column's $q$ (Left) makes Row indifferent: Up gives $3q + 6(1 - q)$, Down gives $2q + 9(1 - q)$. Equal when $6 - 3q = 9 - 7q$, so $q = 3/4$.
blocks.a: Row plays Up with probability $5/6$; Column plays Left with probability $3/4$.

blocks.title: A penalty kick
blocks.q: Scoring chances: kick left & dive left 30%, kick left & dive right 80%, kick right & dive left 90%, kick right & dive right 30%. How often does the kicker go left?
steps: The kicker's mix $x$ must make the goalie indifferent: diving left allows $30x + 90(1 - x)$, diving right $80x + 30(1 - x)$.

The kicker goes left a bit more than half the time. Right kicks are deadlier when the goalie guesses wrong (90% against 80%), so if the kicker went right half the time the goalie would simply guard the right. Aiming left a little more often keeps the goalie guessing.

blocks.html: Finding a player's mixing probabilities from that player's own payoffs. In the first example, using Row's own payoffs to set Row's $p$ would give $3/4$, which is really Column's equilibrium mix. Check: after you find $p$, plug it into the other player's two expected payoffs. They must come out equal.
More on randomizing, including zero-sum games, in Mixed Strategies and Zero-Sum Games.

blocks.html: In many games players move in turn and can see what came before: a firm decides whether to enter, then the incumbent decides how to respond. Best Responses and Nash Equilibrium still applies, but timing lets us find which equilibria make sense.

Solve a game tree by backward induction: start at the last decisions, pick each mover's best choice there, carry those payoffs up, and repeat until the first move. The result is a subgame-perfect equilibrium. It rules out empty threats: plans a player would not actually carry out when the time came.

At the last move nothing follows, so the mover simply takes the best payoff. One step earlier, the mover knows exactly what will happen after each choice, so she compares those known outcomes. Working up the tree this way gives every player a choice that is best at every point where they might have to move, even points that are never reached. A threat that would hurt the threatener if carried out fails that test, so a forward-looking rival ignores it.

blocks.name: ec-gametree
blocks.cap: An entry game. Press Solve to walk backward from the incumbent's choice to the entrant's. Show the threat to see why "I will fight" is not believable.

blocks.title: An entry game
blocks.q: Stay out: (entrant 0, incumbent 100). Enter, then Fight: (−10, 20). Enter, then Accommodate: (30, 40).
steps: Last move: after entry the incumbent compares 20 (Fight) with 40 (Accommodate) and accommodates.
First move: the entrant compares 30 (Enter, knowing it will be accommodated) with 0 (Stay out) and enters.
Subgame-perfect outcome: Enter, then Accommodate, payoffs (30, 40).

blocks.title: The empty threat
blocks.q: In the same game, (Stay out, "Fight if you enter") is a Nash equilibrium of the matrix form. Why isn't it subgame perfect?
steps: If the entrant believes the threat, staying out is a best response, and the incumbent's threat costs it nothing because it never has to act.
But if entry did happen, fighting would give the incumbent 20 instead of 40. It would not fight.
Backward induction removes plans that are not best at the moment they would be carried out.

blocks.html: Solving the tree from the top down, or believing a threat that would hurt the player who carries it out. At the first move you can't know what is best until you know what will follow, so always start at the end. Check: at every decision point in your answer, is the mover choosing her best payoff given what follows? If not, the plan is not subgame perfect.

Commitment can make a threat credible by changing the payoffs in advance, for example an incumbent that builds extra capacity before entry, so that fighting a price war becomes its best response. That is the leader's advantage in Stackelberg Leadership.
Work through more trees in Sequential Games and Backward Induction.

blocks.html: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, cheating is a dominant strategy. Yet firms in a cartel, countries in a trade agreement and neighbors often cooperate for years. Sequential Games and Backward Induction and Infinite Geometric Series explain when.

In a game repeated with no known last round, cooperation can be an equilibrium if players value the future enough. With stage payoffs $T > R > P$ (temptation, reward for cooperating, punishment) and the grim trigger strategy (cooperate until the other cheats, then cheat forever), cooperation is sustainable when $$\frac{R}{1 - \delta} \ge T + \frac{\delta P}{1 - \delta}, \quad\text{that is,}\quad \delta \ge \frac{T - R}{T - P}.$$

Cooperating forever pays $R + R\delta + R\delta^2 + \cdots = \dfrac{R}{1 - \delta}$. Cheating pays $T$ once, then the punishment $P$ in every later round: $T + \dfrac{\delta P}{1 - \delta}$. Multiply both by $1 - \delta$ and rearrange: $R \ge (1 - \delta)T + \delta P$, which gives the threshold. A high $\delta$ (patient players, or a high chance the game continues) makes future losses loom large. If the game has a known last round, cooperation unravels: in the last round cheating is best, so in the round before nothing can be gained by cooperating, and so on back to the start.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: A cartel's pricing game repeated. Move the discount factor: once it passes the threshold $\delta^*$, the value of keeping the agreement beats a one-time gain from cheating followed by a price war.

blocks.title: Finding the threshold
blocks.q: $T = 10$, $R = 6$, $P = 2$. When can grim trigger sustain cooperation?
steps: At $\delta = 0.8$: cooperating is worth $\dfrac{6}{0.2} = 30$; cheating is worth $10 + \dfrac{2(0.8)}{0.2} = 18$. Cooperate.
At $\delta = 0.4$: cooperating is worth 10; cheating is worth $10 + \dfrac{0.8}{0.6} \approx 11.33$. Cheat.

blocks.title: A known last round
blocks.q: The same game is played exactly 5 times, and both players know it. Can cooperation last?
steps: Round 5 is a one-shot game: both cheat.
In round 4, round 5's outcome is fixed whatever happens, so round 4 is effectively one-shot too: both cheat.
The argument repeats back to round 1. With a known end, the subgame-perfect outcome is cheating every round.
blocks.a: No: it unravels from the end.

blocks.html: Thinking a big payoff from cooperating is enough. What matters is the comparison: the one-time gain from cheating, $T - R$, against the future loss from punishment, $R - P$ in every later round, weighted by $\delta$. Check: compute $\delta^*$ and compare it with the discount factor, not just $R$ with $P$.

The discount factor combines patience with the chance that the game continues: if each round is followed by another with probability 0.9 and money is discounted at 0.95 per round, $\delta = 0.9 \times 0.95 = 0.855$. Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments (1980s) found that simple reciprocating strategies such as tit-for-tat did well in repeated prisoner's dilemmas.
Experiment with strategies in Repeated Games and Cooperation.

blocks.html: In an oligopoly a few firms each know that their own output moves the price. Cournot's model treats quantities as the choice and looks for a Nash equilibrium. Each firm solves a small version of Monopoly with Calculus: a monopoly over the demand left over by its rival.

With inverse demand $P = a - b(q_1 + q_2)$ and marginal costs $c_1, c_2$, firm 1's best response to $q_2$ is $$q_1 = \frac{a - c_1 - bq_2}{2b}.$$ The Cournot equilibrium solves both best responses at once: $q_1 = \dfrac{a - 2c_1 + c_2}{3b}$. With equal costs each firm makes $\dfrac{a - c}{3b}$, and total output lies between the monopoly and competitive levels.

Firm 1 takes $q_2$ as fixed and maximizes $(a - bq_1 - bq_2)q_1 - c_1q_1$. Its marginal revenue is $a - 2bq_1 - bq_2$: like a monopoly facing the residual demand $a - bq_2 - bq_1$. Setting it equal to $c_1$ gives the best response. Each firm's best response falls as its rival produces more. The equilibrium is where the two best-response lines cross. Each firm ignores the fact that its extra output also lowers its rival's profit, so together they produce more than a monopoly (or a cartel) would.

blocks.name: linesystem
blocks.cap: Best responses for $P = 100 - Q$ and $c = 10$, with $q_1$ across and $q_2$ up. Firm 1's: $q_1 = 45 - q_2/2$, drawn as $q_2 = 90 - 2q_1$. Firm 2's: $q_2 = 45 - q_1/2$. They cross at (30, 30).

blocks.title: Symmetric duopoly
blocks.q: $P = 100 - Q$, $c = 10$ for both firms.
steps: Best response: $q_1 = \dfrac{90 - q_2}{2}$. By symmetry $q_1 = q_2 = q$, so $q = \dfrac{90 - q}{2}$ and $q = 30$.
Compare: a monopoly makes 45 at \$55 (profit 2,025); competition ($P = MC$) makes 90 at \$10.

blocks.title: Different costs
steps: The low-cost firm produces more and earns more, but the high-cost firm still produces: unlike Bertrand competition, it isn't driven out.

blocks.html: Maximizing each firm's profit as if it were a monopoly, leaving the rival's output out of the price. That gives each firm the monopoly quantity (45 above), a total of 90 and a price of 10: neither firm's choice is a best response to the other's. Check: plug your $q_2$ into firm 1's best response; you must get back your $q_1$.

blocks.html: Cournot Competition had firms choose quantities. If instead they choose prices, the answer changes dramatically, at least when the products are identical.

Two firms selling identical goods with the same constant marginal cost and no capacity limits, choosing prices at the same time, end up with $$p = MC$$ and zero profit (the Bertrand paradox). With different costs $c_1 < c_2$, the low-cost firm prices just below $c_2$ and serves the whole market. With differentiated products, prices stay above cost.

Suppose both charge the same price above marginal cost and split the market. Either firm could cut its price by a cent and take the whole market, nearly doubling its profit. So no price above cost is stable. Below cost, a firm loses money on every sale and would rather raise its price. Only $p = MC$ survives. If products differ, a small price cut steals only some customers, and best responses settle above cost: with demand $q_i = A - p_i + e\,p_j$ (where $0 < e < 1$), firm $i$'s best response is $p_i = \dfrac{A + c + e\,p_j}{2}$.

blocks.name: linesystem
blocks.cap: Price best responses with differentiated products: $q_i = 35 - p_i + \tfrac{1}{2}p_j$, $c = 10$. Firm 1's best response $p_1 = 22.5 + p_2/4$ is drawn as $p_2 = 4p_1 - 90$; firm 2's is $p_2 = 22.5 + p_1/4$. They cross at \$30, well above the \$10 cost.

blocks.title: Identical goods
blocks.q: Two firms sell identical cement with $MC = 40$.
steps: At any common price above 40, undercutting by a cent takes the whole market.

blocks.title: Different costs
steps: Firm 2 won't sell below 30. Firm 1 can price at \$29.99, serve the market and earn almost $(30 - 20)(70) = 700$.
Firm 1's monopoly price would be $(100 + 20)/2 = 60$, above 30, so it doesn't want to go higher than 30 either: it would lose the market to firm 2.

blocks.html: Expecting two firms to keep prices well above cost, as in Cournot. With identical products, price competition, equal costs and no capacity limits, undercutting continues until $P = MC$. Check which assumption a real market breaks before predicting high prices: products that differ, capacity limits, or repeated play (see Repeated Games and Cooperation) can all keep prices up.

Capacity matters: if firms first choose how much capacity to build and then compete on price, the outcome can look like Cournot (a result due to David Kreps and José Scheinkman, 1983). Cournot and Bertrand are two ends of a range, and which fits depends on the industry.
See both models side by side in Competition: Cournot, Bertrand and Hotelling.

blocks.html: What if one firm moves first? A leader that commits to its output, knowing the follower will react, plays a sequential version of Cournot Competition, solved by Sequential Games and Backward Induction.

With $P = a - b(q_L + q_F)$ and common cost $c$, the follower plays its Cournot best response $q_F = \dfrac{a - c - bq_L}{2b}$. The leader, anticipating this, produces $$q_L = \frac{a - c}{2b}, \qquad q_F = \frac{a - c}{4b}.$$ The leader produces more and earns more than in Cournot; the follower produces less and earns less.

Backward induction: the follower moves last, so its choice is its best response to whatever $q_L$ it sees. The leader substitutes that response into the price before maximizing: $$P = a - bq_L - b\cdot\frac{a - c - bq_L}{2b} = \frac{a + c - bq_L}{2}.$$ Its profit is $\left(\dfrac{a + c - bq_L}{2} - c\right)q_L = \dfrac{(a - c - bq_L)q_L}{2}$, maximized at $q_L = \dfrac{a - c}{2b}$. Moving first is valuable because the leader's big output is a commitment: the follower can only accept it and shrink.

blocks.name: ec-gametree
blocks.cap: A Stackelberg game as a tree: the leader chooses a quantity, the follower responds. Walking backward picks the follower's best reply at each node, then the leader's best choice.

blocks.title: Leader and follower
steps: Cournot gave each 900: the leader gains 112.5, the follower loses 393.75, and total output rises from 60 to 67.5.

blocks.title: Why not just announce a big number?
blocks.q: In Cournot (moving at the same time), firm 1 says it will produce 45. Is that believable?
steps: If firm 2 believed it, firm 2 would produce 22.5; but firm 1's best response to 22.5 is $\dfrac{90 - 22.5}{2} = 33.75$, not 45.
Without a way to commit first, the announcement is not credible. Stackelberg leadership requires that the leader's choice really is made, and seen, first.
blocks.a: No: only a real first move commits.

blocks.html: Giving the leader its Cournot best response, as if it ignored the follower's reaction. The leader's advantage comes from substituting $q_F(q_L)$ into its profit before maximizing. Check: compute the leader's profit at your answer and at the Cournot quantity; the Stackelberg choice must be at least as good for the leader.

blocks.html: Auctions sell spectrum licenses, artwork, ad slots and government bonds. Their rules are games, and the ideas from Best Responses and Nash Equilibrium and Payoff Matrices and Dominant Strategies predict how people bid.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction (highest bid wins, pays the second-highest bid), bidding your true value is a dominant strategy. In a first-price auction (winner pays her own bid), bidders shade their bids; with $n$ bidders whose values are independent and uniform, the equilibrium bid is $b(v) = \dfrac{n - 1}{n}v$. With values uniform on $[0, V]$, both formats give the seller the same expected revenue, $\dfrac{n - 1}{n + 1}V$ (revenue equivalence).

In a second-price auction your bid decides only whether you win; the price is set by someone else's bid $B$. Bidding your value $v$ wins exactly when $B < v$, the cases where winning is profitable. Bidding less can only lose some of those profitable wins; bidding more can only add wins at prices above $v$. In a first-price auction your bid is your price, so you trade a lower chance of winning for a bigger margin, and you shade more when there are fewer rivals.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Equilibrium first-price bids with $n$ bidders and values uniform on [0, 100]. With 2 bidders each bids half her value; as $n$ grows, bids approach values.

blocks.title: Second price
blocks.q: Sealed bids: Ana \$120, Ben \$90, Chloe \$75. Ana's value is \$130.
steps: Ana wins and pays the second-highest bid, \$90.
Her surplus: $130 - 90 = 40$. Had she bid \$100 or \$200, she would still win and still pay \$90.

blocks.title: First price
blocks.q: Four bidders, values uniform on [0, 100]. What does a bidder with value 80 bid, and what is the seller's expected revenue?
steps: Expected revenue: $\dfrac{4 - 1}{4 + 1}(100) = 60$, the same as in a second-price auction, where the price is the expected second-highest value.

blocks.html: Shading your bid in a second-price auction "to keep some surplus." Your surplus there is your value minus the second bid, which your own bid doesn't change. Shading only matters when it makes you lose an auction you would have won at a price below your value. Check: compare the outcome of bidding your value with any other bid for every possible highest rival bid; truthful bidding is never worse.

William Vickrey analyzed the second-price auction in 1961. Revenue equivalence needs strong assumptions (independent private values, risk-neutral bidders, symmetric bidders); when they fail, for example with risk-averse bidders, first-price auctions tend to raise more.

blocks.html: Until now one consumer faced fixed prices. General equilibrium asks how a whole economy's goods end up divided. The simplest case has two people and two goods, and a picture that puts both people's indifference maps (often from the Cobb-Douglas family) in one box.

In an Edgeworth box with $X$ units of $x$ and $Y$ units of $y$, every point is an allocation: A's bundle measured from the bottom-left corner, B's from the top-right. An allocation is Pareto efficient if no change can make one person better off without making the other worse off. At an interior efficient allocation the two indifference curves are tangent: $$MRS_A = MRS_B.$$ The set of efficient allocations is the contract curve.

Suppose $MRS_A = 3$ and $MRS_B = 1/3$: A would give up 3 units of $y$ for one more $x$, while B would give up a unit of $x$ for just $1/3$ of a $y$. Let B give A one unit of $x$ in exchange for one unit of $y$: A pays less than her limit of 3 and B gets more than his limit of $1/3$. Both gain. In the picture, the two indifference curves through the allocation form a lens; every allocation inside it is better for both. Only where the curves touch, and the lens disappears, is there no such trade left.

blocks.name: ec-edgeworth
blocks.cap: Both people have $U = \sqrt{xy}$ and 20 units of each good. A starts with (5, 15). The lens between their indifference curves holds every allocation both prefer; the contract curve is the diagonal.

blocks.title: An inefficient allocation
blocks.q: $X = Y = 20$; both have $U = xy$. A has (5, 15), so B has (15, 5). Is this efficient?
steps: They differ, so a trade can help both: B gives A some $x$ for $y$ at any rate between $1/3$ and 3.
For instance A gives 2 of $y$ for 2 of $x$: A moves to (7, 13), utility $91 > 75$; B moves to (13, 7), utility $91 > 75$.

blocks.title: Finding a point on the contract curve
blocks.q: $X = Y = 30$. $U_A = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$ and $U_B = x^{1/3}y^{2/3}$. If A has 10 units of $x$ at an efficient allocation, how much $y$ does A have?

blocks.html: Thinking Pareto efficient means fair. The corner where A has everything is efficient: any change gives B something only by taking it from A. Efficiency rules out waste; it says nothing about how the total is shared. Check: to judge fairness you need a separate standard (equality, need, desert); the contract curve contains both very equal and very unequal allocations.

blocks.html: In the The Edgeworth Box and Pareto Efficiency, where do the two people end up if they trade at market prices? Each acts like the consumer of Cobb-Douglas Demand, with one twist: their income is not a fixed number of dollars.

A competitive equilibrium is a price ratio at which each person, choosing the best bundle she can afford with the value of her endowment, demands amounts that together use up exactly what exists. With $y$ as money ($p_y = 1$) and $p$ the price of $x$: income $m_i = p\,\omega_{ix} + \omega_{iy}$, and the market for $x$ clears. By Walras's law, when one market clears the other does too.

Each person's spending equals the value of what she brings, so total spending equals the total value of all endowments. If the $x$ market clears, the value of $x$ bought equals the value of $x$ available, so the leftover spending on $y$ must equal the value of $y$ available: the $y$ market clears too. And only relative prices matter: doubling every price doubles every income and changes nothing. That is why we can set $p_y = 1$. In the box, the price line passes through the endowment with slope $-p$, and equilibrium is where both people's best points on that line coincide.

blocks.name: ec-edgeworth

opts.task: Move the price slider until the two demanded bundles meet, or press the button that finds the equilibrium.

blocks.cap: The price line through the endowment (20, 10). At the wrong price the two people demand bundles that don't fit together: one market has excess demand, the other excess supply.

blocks.title: Identical preferences
steps: Demands for $x$: $x_A = \dfrac{m_A}{2p}$ and $x_B = \dfrac{m_B}{2p}$. Clearing: $\dfrac{30p + 30}{2p} = 30$, so $30p + 30 = 60p$ and $p = 1$.

blocks.title: Different tastes
blocks.q: $U_A = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$ with endowment (10, 0); $U_B = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$ with endowment (0, 30).
steps: A: income 15, buys $x_A = 5$ and $y_A = 7.5$. B: buys $x_B = 5$ and $y_B = 22.5$. Both markets clear.

blocks.html: Treating income as a fixed number of dollars. Here income is the value of the endowment at the price you are solving for, so it changes as $p$ changes. Writing $x_A = \tfrac{1}{2}m_A/p$ with $m_A$ held fixed gives the wrong clearing equation. Check: write each income as $p\,\omega_x + \omega_y$ before you set up the market-clearing condition.

blocks.html: Two results connect the Competitive Equilibrium in Exchange to the efficiency idea of Allocative and Productive Efficiency. They are the formal core of the case for markets, and also of the case for redistributing through transfers rather than by fixing prices.

First welfare theorem: with price-taking behavior, complete markets, no externalities and full information, every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Second welfare theorem: with convex preferences as well, any Pareto-efficient allocation can be reached as a competitive equilibrium after suitable lump-sum transfers of wealth.

In the box: at a competitive equilibrium each person's indifference curve is tangent to the same price line, so $MRS_A = p = MRS_B$, which is the efficiency condition. The general argument: if some other allocation made someone better off and no one worse off, it would have to cost more than her budget for the better-off person and at least as much for everyone else, at the equilibrium prices, so its total value would exceed the value of everything that exists. That is impossible. For the second theorem, pick an efficient point; the common tangent line through it is a price line; move wealth by lump sums so that each person can just afford her part of the point; then at those prices each chooses exactly that part.

blocks.name: ec-edgeworth
blocks.cap: The competitive equilibrium from any endowment lands on the contract curve. Moving the endowment (a lump-sum transfer) moves the equilibrium along the curve.

blocks.title: A transfer that picks the outcome
blocks.q: Both have $U = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}$; there are 100 units of each good; A starts with (30, 40). Which transfer (in units of $y$) makes A end up with (60, 60) in equilibrium?
steps: With identical Cobb-Douglas tastes the contract curve is the diagonal and the equilibrium price is $p = \dfrac{1/2}{1/2}\cdot\dfrac{100}{100} = 1$, whatever the endowments.
To choose (60, 60) at $p = 1$, A needs wealth 120.
A's endowment is worth $30 + 40 = 70$, so the transfer is $+50$ units of $y$ from B to A.

blocks.title: When the first theorem fails
blocks.q: A factory's smoke harms nearby residents, who are not part of any market for it. Does the competitive equilibrium have to be efficient?
steps: No. The theorem needs no externalities: here the factory's choice affects others without a price.
The market produces where private benefit equals private cost, ignoring the damage (see The Efficient Amount of an Externality).
blocks.a: No: an externality breaks the theorem's conditions.

blocks.html: Reading the first welfare theorem as "markets give fair results," or forgetting its conditions. It promises efficiency only, and only with price-taking, complete markets, no externalities and full information. Check: before invoking it, list the conditions and ask whether each holds. Market power, pollution, public goods and hidden information are the usual exceptions, and Unit 10 takes them up.

What economists broadly agree on: the theorems are benchmarks that explain why markets often allocate goods well and where they can fail. What they debate: real redistribution can't use true lump-sum transfers (taxes on income or spending change behavior), so separating efficiency from fairness has a cost, and how large that cost is, and how much redistribution is worth it, are open questions.

blocks.html: Correcting Externalities showed that a tax equal to the marginal external cost can fix overproduction. With the supply side from The Competitive Firm's Supply Curve and a little calculus, we can find exactly how big the tax should be and how much the uncorrected market wastes.

With marginal benefit $MB(Q)$ (demand), marginal private cost $MPC(Q)$ (supply) and marginal external cost $MEC(Q)$, the efficient quantity solves $$MB(Q^*) = MSC(Q^*) = MPC(Q^*) + MEC(Q^*).$$ A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external damage at the efficient quantity, $t = MEC(Q^*)$, moves the market there.

Total surplus counting everyone is $W(Q) = \int_0^Q \big(MB - MPC - MEC\big)\,dq$. Its derivative is $MB - MPC - MEC$, which is zero at $Q^*$. The market stops where $MB = MPC$, past $Q^*$, because no buyer or seller pays for the damage. With a tax $t$, sellers act as if marginal cost were $MPC + t$; choosing $t = MEC(Q^*)$ makes $MPC + t$ cross $MB$ exactly at $Q^*$. Each unit between $Q^*$ and the market quantity costs society more than it is worth; adding up that gap gives the deadweight loss.

blocks.name: ec-externality

opts.task: Raise the tax until the market lands on the efficient quantity.

blocks.cap: Marginal social cost lies above supply by the marginal external cost. The hatched triangle is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market; the right tax removes it.

blocks.title: The wrong tax
blocks.q: What if the tax were set at the marginal damage at the market quantity, $MEC(40) = 30$?
steps: The market would solve $100 - Q = 50 + Q$: $Q = 25$, below the efficient 28.
The damage per unit falls as output falls, so taxing at the old, higher damage overshoots.

blocks.html: Setting the tax equal to the marginal damage at the market quantity. That is where the damage is measured before the policy, but the tax should reflect the damage where the market will end up. Check: plug your tax into $MB = MPC + t$ and solve. You must get $Q^*$.

The efficient amount of pollution is usually not zero: cutting the last units of damage would cost more than it saves. Economists broadly agree that pricing pollution (by taxes or tradable permits) reaches a given cut at lower cost than rules that tell every firm what to do; measuring the damage, and choosing among those tools in practice, involve debates about evidence and values.

blocks.html: The Efficient Amount of an Externality fixed an externality with a tax. Ronald Coase (1960) pointed out that when only a few parties are involved, they may fix it themselves by bargaining, as long as the law says clearly who has which right.

Coase theorem: with clear property rights, costless bargaining and no income effects, the parties reach the efficient amount of the harmful activity whoever holds the right. The assignment of the right decides only who pays whom.

Let the activity's marginal benefit to its owner be $MB(Q)$ and the marginal damage to the neighbor $MD(Q)$. If the owner has the right and would choose more than $Q^*$, each extra unit beyond $Q^*$ is worth less to the owner than it costs the neighbor, so the neighbor can pay the owner to cut back and both gain. If the neighbor has the right and would allow nothing, each unit up to $Q^*$ is worth more to the owner than it costs the neighbor, so the owner can pay for permission. Either way, bargaining stops at $Q^*$, where $MB = MD$. The payment lies between what the giving side loses and what the receiving side gains.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: A factory's benefit from smoke and a laundry's damage. They cross at $Q^* = 10$. The shaded area between 10 and 15 is the net gain from cutting back from the factory's preferred 15 units to 10.

blocks.title: The efficient amount and the payments
blocks.q: $MB = 30 - 2Q$ for the factory, $MD = Q$ for the laundry. The factory has the right to pollute.
steps: Efficient: $30 - 2Q = Q$, so $Q^* = 10$. On its own the factory would go to $Q = 15$ (where $MB = 0$).
Any payment from the laundry between \$25 and \$62.50 makes both better off; they settle at 10.

blocks.title: The other assignment
blocks.q: Now the laundry has the right to clean air.
steps: Starting from $Q = 0$, allowing 10 units costs the laundry $\int_0^{10}Q\,dQ = 50$ and is worth $\int_0^{10}(30 - 2Q)\,dQ = 200$ to the factory.
The factory pays between \$50 and \$200, and again $Q = 10$.

blocks.html: Thinking the efficient amount depends on who holds the right. With costless bargaining and no income effects, it doesn't: both assignments led to 10 units. What changes is the direction of the payment, which matters a great deal to the two parties' wealth. Check: compute $Q^*$ from $MB = MD$ alone; the legal rule should never enter that equation.

The theorem's conditions are demanding. Bargaining costs rise with the number of people affected (a factory and a million neighbors can't easily negotiate), and holdouts, unclear rights and large income effects can block or change the outcome. Coase's own emphasis was that because real transaction costs are often high, the legal assignment of rights matters for efficiency in practice.

blocks.html: Public Goods and Free Riders explained why markets supply too little of goods that no one can be kept from and that everyone uses at once. With The Marginal Rate of Substitution we can state exactly how much is efficient, a rule Paul Samuelson gave in 1954.

For a public good $G$ with marginal cost $MC$, the efficient amount satisfies the Samuelson condition $$\sum_i MB_i(G) = MC(G).$$ Because everyone uses the same units, individual marginal benefits are added vertically (at each quantity), not horizontally as for private goods.

One more unit of a streetlight program lights the street for everyone at once. Its value to society is the sum of what each person would pay for that unit: $MB_1 + MB_2 + \cdots$. Efficiency adds units while that sum exceeds the cost. Compare a private good, where one more unit goes to one person and markets add quantities at a price (Adding Up to Market Demand). If each person decides alone how much to contribute, she stops where her own marginal benefit equals the cost, ignoring the benefit to others, so voluntary contributions fall short: free riding.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Two people's marginal benefits and their vertical sum. The sum crosses the cost of \$23 at $G^* = 9$. On her own, person 2 would stop at 3.5 and person 1 would buy none.

blocks.title: The efficient amount
steps: Both are positive for $G < 15$, so there $\sum MB = 50 - 3G$.
At 9: $MB_1 = 11$, $MB_2 = 12$, summing to 23. Charging each person her own marginal benefit (a Lindahl price) would cover the cost exactly.

blocks.title: Free riding
blocks.q: Same people, but each decides alone how much to buy.
steps: Person 1: $20 - G \ge 23$ never holds, so she buys nothing on her own.
At 3.5, person 1's benefit (16.5 per unit) is below the cost, so she adds nothing and rides free. Total: 3.5, far below 9.

blocks.html: Adding demand curves horizontally, as for private goods. That would answer "how many units would they buy in total at a price of \$23," treating each unit as consumed by one person. For a public good every unit serves both, so add the heights (willingness to pay) at each quantity. Check: at your answer, the marginal benefits of all users should add up to the marginal cost.

The hard part in practice is learning the $MB_i$: if a person's share of the bill depends on what she reports, she has a reason to understate her benefit. Governments fund public goods through taxes, and economists study mechanisms that make honest reporting worthwhile.

blocks.html: A fishery, a groundwater basin or a grazing commons is rival (my catch leaves less for you) but hard to fence off (see Rival and Excludable Goods). Like the polluter in The Efficient Amount of an Externality, each user imposes a cost on others that no one pays for.

If $N$ users of a common resource produce total output $Y(N)$ and each pays cost $c$, open access draws users until the average product covers the cost, $Y(N)/N = c$. The efficient number sets the marginal product equal to the cost, $Y'(N) = c$. Because adding users lowers everyone's average catch, open access overuses the resource and wipes out its value (the rent).

A new boat catches the average catch, $AP = Y/N$, so it joins as long as $AP \ge c$. But its arrival lowers every other boat's catch a little, so the total rises only by the marginal product $Y'(N)$, which is less than the average when the resource is crowded. The boat's owner ignores the loss to others: an externality. The efficient number maximizes total catch minus total cost, $Y(N) - cN$, which needs $Y'(N) = c$. A license fee equal to $AP - c$ at the efficient number, or a cap on boats or catch, closes the gap.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Catch $Y(N) = 100N - N^2$ (thousand dollars), cost 20 per boat. Open access stops where average catch meets cost, at 80 boats; the efficient number is where marginal catch meets cost, at 40.

blocks.title: Open access versus efficient use
blocks.q: $Y(N) = 100N - N^2$ (thousand dollars), $c = 20$.
steps: Rent at 40: $Y = 4{,}000 - 1{,}600 = 2{,}400$, minus costs 800: 1,600 thousand dollars a season, all lost under open access.
blocks.a: 80 boats under open access; 40 is efficient.

blocks.title: A license fee
blocks.q: What fee per boat brings open access down to 40 boats?
steps: With fee $F$, boats enter until $AP = 20 + F$.
Total fees, $40 \times 40 = 1{,}600$, collect exactly the rent that open access would have wasted.

blocks.html: Expecting open access to give efficient use because each user is rational. Each user is rational about her own costs and catch, but ignores the catch she takes from others. Check: compare average and marginal product at the open-access number. If $MP$ is below the cost there, the last boats are destroying value.

Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay called overuse "the tragedy of the commons." Elinor Ostrom's research, recognized with a Nobel prize in 2009, documented many communities that manage shared resources well with their own rules, monitoring and sanctions. Overuse is a risk of open access, not a law of nature.

blocks.html: In Insurance the insurer knew each buyer's risk. Often one side of a deal knows more. With the market model of Market Equilibrium, hidden information can make a market shrink or vanish.

Adverse selection: when one side knows the quality (or risk) before the deal and the other can't tell, the price reflects only the average, so the best types may refuse to trade. The goods (or customers) left in the market are worse on average, which pushes the price down further. George Akerlof (1970) called it the market for "lemons."

Suppose a share $\pi$ of used cars are good and the rest are lemons, and buyers can't tell them apart. A risk-neutral buyer will pay at most the average value, $\pi B_g + (1 - \pi)B_l$. If that is below what owners of good cars require, $S_g$, those owners keep their cars. Buyers then know that only lemons are for sale, and pay at most $B_l$. Trades that would help both sides (a good car is worth more to a buyer than to its owner) never happen. The same logic hits insurance: at a price set for average risk, low-risk people may drop out, raising the average risk of those who remain.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Across: $\pi$, the share of good cars. Up: thousands of dollars. Good cars are worth \$6,000 to buyers and lemons \$2,000, so a random car is worth $2 + 4\pi$ thousand; good-car owners need \$5,000. Only when at least 3/4 of cars are good does a random car's value reach that.

blocks.title: Does the market for good cars survive?
blocks.q: Half the cars are good. Buyers value good cars at \$6,000 and lemons at \$2,000; owners of good cars need \$5,000; owners of lemons need \$1,000.
steps: A random car is worth $\tfrac{1}{2}(6{,}000) + \tfrac{1}{2}(2{,}000) = 4{,}000$ to a buyer.
That is below the \$5,000 good-car owners need, so they don't sell.
Only lemons trade, at a price between \$1,000 and \$2,000, even though every good car is worth \$1,000 more to a buyer than to its owner.

blocks.title: The threshold
blocks.q: Same values. What share of good cars keeps them in the market?

blocks.html: Mixing up adverse selection with moral hazard. Adverse selection is hidden information that exists before the deal (the car's quality, the buyer's health); it changes who trades. Moral hazard is a hidden action after the deal (driving carelessly once insured). Check: ask whether the problem would exist even if everyone's behavior stayed the same after signing. If yes, it is adverse selection.

Markets and governments respond in several ways: warranties and inspections, reputations and reviews, signals (next lessons), pricing by observable risk, and in some insurance markets rules that require or encourage broad participation. Which mix works best in a given market is a matter of evidence and debate.
See how beliefs about hidden types work in Incomplete Information and Bayesian Games.

blocks.html: Insurance protects people from losses, but it can also change what they do. When one side's actions after a deal are hidden, the other side bears costs it can't control.

Moral hazard: a person changes her hidden behavior after a deal because someone else now bears part of the cost. Contracts restore incentives by leaving some of the cost with her: deductibles, copays and coinsurance for insurance, and pay tied to results (bonuses, commissions) for work. The price is that she bears some risk again.

With full insurance, a careful driver pays the cost of care but the insurer gets all the savings from fewer accidents, so care doesn't pay. If the driver keeps a deductible $D$ per accident, care cuts her expected losses by $(\pi_H - \pi_L)D$, where $\pi_H$ and $\pi_L$ are the accident chances without and with care. Care is worth it when that saving covers its cost $c$: $$D \ge \frac{c}{\pi_H - \pi_L}.$$ The same incentive condition sets the smallest bonus that makes hidden effort worthwhile at work.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The driver's expected yearly cost against the deductible $D$. Careless: $0.2D$. Careful: \$60 of care plus $0.1D$. Below a \$600 deductible carelessness is cheaper for the driver; above it, care is.

blocks.title: The smallest deductible
blocks.q: Care costs the equivalent of \$60 a year and lowers the yearly accident chance from 0.2 to 0.1.

blocks.title: A bonus for hidden effort
blocks.q: Extra effort costs a salesperson the equivalent of \$200 and raises her chance of landing a client from 0.4 to 0.8. What bonus for landing the client makes effort worth it?
steps: Effort raises the expected bonus by $(0.8 - 0.4)B = 0.4B$.

blocks.html: Calling any risky behavior moral hazard. A skydiver who loves risk and pays her own costs is not an example: no one else bears the consequences of her choice. Moral hazard needs a deal that shifts costs to someone else and an action that party can't see. Check: who pays for the bad outcome, and could they observe the behavior?

The trade-off is real: deductibles and performance pay improve incentives but make people bear risk they would rather insure, so the best contract balances the two. How large moral hazard effects are in health care and other markets is measured in many studies, with results that vary by setting.

blocks.html: Adverse Selection and Lemons showed hidden information driving good types out. Sometimes the good types can fight back by doing something the bad types find too costly to copy. Michael Spence's 1973 model of job-market signaling shows how, using equilibrium reasoning.

A costly action can separate types when it costs the high type less than the low type. With wages $w_H$ and $w_L$ and per-year costs of education $c_H < c_L$, a requirement of $e^*$ years separates the types when $$\frac{w_H - w_L}{c_L} \le e^* \le \frac{w_H - w_L}{c_H}.$$ The signal works even if it adds nothing to productivity.

Employers pay $w_H$ to anyone with at least $e^*$ years. A low type compares copying, $w_H - c_Le^*$, with not copying, $w_L$; she won't copy if $e^* \ge (w_H - w_L)/c_L$. A high type compares $w_H - c_He^*$ with $w_L$; she gets the education if $e^* \le (w_H - w_L)/c_H$. Because $c_H < c_L$, there is a range of $e^*$ that satisfies both, and then employers' beliefs are confirmed: everyone with the credential is high-productivity. The key is the cost difference (economists call it single crossing), not what the education teaches.

blocks.title: The separating range
blocks.q: $w_H = 70$, $w_L = 40$ (thousand dollars), $c_H = 5$, $c_L = 10$ per year.
steps: Any requirement from 3 to 6 years separates the types.

blocks.title: Testing requirements
blocks.q: Same numbers. Do $e^* = 2$, $4$ and $7$ separate?
steps: $e^* = 2$: a low type gets $70 - 20 = 50 > 40$, so she copies. No separation.
$e^* = 4$: low type $70 - 40 = 30 < 40$ (won't copy); high type $70 - 20 = 50 > 40$ (signals). Separates.
$e^* = 7$: high type $70 - 35 = 35 < 40$: even high types skip it. No separation.

blocks.html: Thinking a signal works only if it raises productivity. In this model education teaches nothing, yet it separates the types, because it costs the low type more than imitating the high type is worth. Check: a proposed signal works when $w_H - w_L$ lies between its total cost to the high type and its total cost to the low type.

How much of education's payoff in the real labor market is signaling and how much is the skills it builds is studied and debated; the evidence suggests both play a part. Signals appear elsewhere too: warranties signal reliable products, and costly advertising can signal a firm's confidence in repeat sales.
